# Steinoak Clause Library — Consolidated Named-Topic Checklist

> **STANDING RULE — NO RE-AUDITS (Taylor, 2026-09-26).** Every completed state (CO, WY, KS, NE, MN, ND, SD, OH, CA, NV, TX, NJ, FL) is closed. **No re-audit of any completed state is planned, now or later.** "Re-audit" means re-scrubbing everything for a state, and that won't happen. Targeted work is welcome: going back to re-verify or fix a specific row or topic in a completed state (a scalpel, not a hammer) needs no special justification; just say what and why. The word "re-audit" throughout these files refers to the one-time settings re-run of Aug–Sep 2026, which is finished. Older phrases such as "flag for the X re-audit", "live item for the X re-audit", "when X is next revisited" or "screen the completed states on their next revisit" are historical and dead: they are not a queue. Do not propose, plan or mention a re-audit, and do not park anything "for the re-audit". If something specific in a completed state looks wrong or unverified, say what and why and propose the targeted fix.

**Purpose:** every state-specific finding logged across Colorado (state #1), Wyoming (state #2), Kansas (state #3), Nebraska (state #4), Minnesota (state #5), North Dakota (state #6), and South Dakota (state #7), consolidated into one list. This is the canvass a new state runs against — per the standing rule (KS log, session 7): check every item below explicitly present/absent for the new state. (The old "run the canvass twice" rule is superseded by instruction 22: one pass at the correct settings.) **Note (2026-09-18):** this header previously said Minnesota wasn't folded in and omitted South Dakota entirely. A full row-by-row read confirmed the main topic tables (through "New topics added by North Dakota") and every re-audit-results section are genuinely populated for all 7 states — that part of the stale claim is corrected. One real, separate staleness problem was found and fixed in the process: the **CORE OBLIGATIONS** section (near the bottom of this file) had a framing note claiming six of seven state columns were `NOT CANVASSED`, when in fact all seven were filled with cited research — see that section's own corrected note for the actual remaining gaps (a handful of specific inline-flagged items, not whole columns). Still worth a sanity check rather than blind trust before Ohio starts (see Instructions item 19), since this file has now demonstrated its prose can lag its own tables more than once. When a new state is completed, its own findings get folded into this list before the next state starts, so this file keeps growing. **OHIO (state #8) FOLDED IN 2026-09-18:** an `OH` column now runs across all ten shared tables, and Ohio's own new-topic section sits immediately above CORE OBLIGATIONS. Ohio was canvassed at the corrected settings from the start — see Instructions item 22, it needs ONE audit, not two. **Nevada sync tasks: done 2026-09-25.** They are listed at the top of `lease-clause-decision-log-NV.md`: propagation notes added to the 8 state logs, and CO metadata restored into the CSV (see instruction 27). **NEVADA (state #10) FOLDED IN 2026-09-24:** an `NV` column now runs across all ten shared tables — After the second text batch (same day: 118A tail, NRS 40.0025–.0045 and 40.215–.425, ch. 118 in full, 202.450–.480, 487.038–.039): After the research-mode pass (same day): **every one of the 69 core rows has an NV answer.** Several are "Not located" with the search boundary stated rather than confirmed absences (CO alarms, immigration status, radon, bed bugs, mold and others — see the NV research section at the end). (The NRS 41.620/597.960 answer was confirmed against revisor text the same day.) The candidate-topic tables were answered for NV the same day (86 refs, end of file). See `lease-clause-decision-log-NV.md` §§11–13.

Code §1934:** where the hiring is **terminable at the pleasure of one of the parties**, it is terminated by notice to the other of that party's death or incapacity to contract; **in all other cases it is not terminated thereby**. My earlier 'not located' entry rested on having read only §1925 and §1933. No CA provision releasing a deceased tenant's estate from a fixed-term lease was found — the base `early-termination` row's death limb was dropped as unverified rather than carried into `early-termination-ca`. Code §1710.2**, which provides that a death on the property need not be disclosed if it occurred **more than three years** before the prospective tenant offers to rent, and never for HIV or AIDS-related death. ## New topics added by the Colorado re-audit (2026-08-27, higher-effort re-run of state #1)

These come from re-auditing CO at Opus/high/research after the original pass was done at default settings. **Every row below is Not Yet Checked for WY, KS, NE, MN, ND, and SD** — none existed when those states ran their canvasses.

| Topic | CO | Check for other states? |
|---|---|---|
| Environmental-event lease termination as an **opt-in** landlord right | **Present — and unusual.** C.R.S. 38-12-503(11) gives the landlord a right to terminate after a sudden environmental public health event or government action rendering occupancy impossible/unlawful, but **only "if permitted by the rental agreement."** A silent lease forfeits the right entirely. | **Yes, high value.** This inverts the usual pattern — most statutes constrain the landlord regardless of lease text; this one grants a right that only exists if you draft for it. Any state with an analogous provision means the library is silently costing landlords a statutory right. |
| Habitability provisions non-waivable **as an entire Part** | **Present.** 38-12-503(10) voids any agreement waiving or modifying *any* right, remedy, obligation, or prohibition in Part 5. Broader than the other four CO non-waiver rules, which each cover a single right. | Yes — check whether other states' habitability chapters carry a blanket non-waiver clause vs. per-right ones. |
| Lease language that **designates verbal notice** waives the landlord's right to written notice | **Present — and it was a live trap in shipped text.** 38-12-503(3)(f)(II). Our `habitability-notice-co` bracket prompt said "e.g. phone, email, or mailing address"; filling in a phone number would have surrendered the written-notice protection. Matters because *Anderson v. Shorter Arms Inv'rs*, 2023 COA 71, holds oral notice insufficient as a matter of law. | **Yes.** Any state where written notice is a strict element may have a parallel self-inflicted-waiver rule. Check every state's habitability-notice clause for a bracket that invites a phone number. |
| Relocation/alternate-housing duty is **tenant-request-triggered**, not automatic | **Present.** 38-12-503(4)(a)(II) — the 24-hour clock runs from the tenant's *request*, not from notice of the condition, and no duty arises absent a request. Prior CO entry had this materially wrong. | Yes — where another state has a relocation duty, confirm the trigger, not just the deadline. |
| Habitability **operational duties** beyond the repair itself | **Present.** 24-hour contact with intentions and estimate; affirmative duty to tell the tenant about the relocation right; records kept tenancy + 3 years, produced within 10 days of request; 72-hour mold containment/HEPA/water-stop protocol; licensed professional required for gas hazards. Several are **independent breach triggers**, not just good practice. | Yes — the original CO pass captured only the response deadlines and missed all of this. Likely the same blind spot in other states. |
| Prohibition on pushing landlord-responsible repairs onto **tenant's renter's insurance** | **Present.** 38-12-503(13) — may not require a tenant to claim on their policy for landlord-responsible remedial costs, nor file against it without express written permission at the time of claim. | Yes. Note every state's `tenants-property-insurance` clause requires coverage — confirm none of them cross this line. |
| **Trained service animal: independent state basis** | **Present.** C.R.S. 24-34-502 (CADA) independently covers assistance animals; HB 21-1271 adds documentation limits and misrepresentation penalties. Does not depend on HUD guidance. | **Yes — split from the ESA row 2026-08-29 (KS re-audit).** Kansas proved a single state can answer these two rows *differently*: KS has a strong independent basis for trained dogs (K.S.A. 39-1102/1107/1108, express housing right, statutory no-fee rule, criminal backing at 39-1103) while **expressly excluding** ESAs. CO and WY collapse to the same answer on both rows, so nothing is lost by splitting; KS is the state that showed the single row was hiding a distinction. **Also check species scope** — KS's statute covers *dogs only*, so a non-canine assistance animal falls outside it entirely. |
| **ESA specifically: independent state basis** | **Present.** CADA's coverage reaches ESAs, not just individually-trained animals. | **Yes — this is the row the HUD change actually threatens.** HUD withdrew its assistance-animal guidance 2025-09-17 and on 2026-05-22 adopted an enforcement standard reaching only individually-trained animals. A state with no independent ESA basis leaves the clause resting on unsettled federal ground → tag NEEDS_REVIEW, not VERIFIED. **Classify each state as: independent animal-specific statute / federally-tethered animal-specific statute / independent but GENERIC accommodation duty / no basis.** The fourth category is new; see the KS row below. **Watch for an adverse cross-current:** a state may have a generic duty that covers ESAs *and* a separate animal-specific statute that expressly excludes them (KS). |
| Source-of-income: **lease-statement duty and acceptance duty have different exemptions** | **Present, and a trap.** 38-12-801(2.5) still exempts landlords with ≤5 single-family homes / ≤5 units from *printing* the statement, but HB25-1240 removed the small-landlord exemption from the *acceptance* mandate in 24-34-502. A small landlord can be exempt from the disclosure while fully bound by the duty. | Yes — where a state has both a statement requirement and an acceptance mandate, check whether their exemptions match. Don't assume one exemption covers both. |
| Rent-increase notice gap on a **written** month-to-month lease | **Present.** 38-12-701(2)'s 60-day notice applies only where there is *no written agreement* — so a written M2M lease silent on notice has no statutory default at all. Resolved by stating a period in the lease. | Yes — check whether other states' rent-increase notice statutes are similarly conditioned on the absence of a written agreement. |
| Lead paint: **Lead Warning Statement must be verbatim** | **Federal, affects all states.** 40 CFR 745.113(b)(1) requires the exact regulatory text; the library had a paraphrase. Corrected 2026-08-27. Also requires the disclosure/records/acknowledgment/certification elements of 745.113(b), and 3-year retention. | **Already applied** — `lead-based-paint` is shared CO;WY;KS;NE;MN and was corrected in place. See propagation note in Open items. |

## New topics added by the Wyoming re-audit (2026-08-28, higher-effort re-run of state #2)

Second state re-audited at higher settings. **Every row below is Not Yet Checked for KS, NE, MN, ND, and SD.**

| Topic | WY | Check for other states? |
|---|---|---|
| **Citation-existence screen** — does the cited section actually exist? | **Found a fabricated cite in shipped lease text.** `assistance-animal-accommodation-wy` cited `Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-207`; the article ends at § 35-13-206. Real section is § 35-13-203(b). Shipped `VERIFIED`, survived a full state pass and two later sessions. The $750 figure was correct — only the section number was invented. | **Yes — run for every state.** Library-wide Tier 1 (citations inside lease clauses) is only 5 rows across all 7 states, and **2 of the 5 carried real errors**. Cheap, mechanical, and it catches a class no amount of careful reading has caught. |
| **A correct citation can still be described wrongly** | CO's `assistance-animal-accommodation-co` called misrepresentation a "criminal offense"; C.R.S. 18-13-107.3 is a **civil infraction**. Cite valid, characterization false. Changed to "is unlawful under". | **Yes.** An existence check cannot catch this. Read what the section *says*, not just that it resolves. |
| **ESA independent state basis — WY resolved PRESENT** | **Present.** Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-201(c) independently bars discrimination in residential leasing "because the person has an assistance animal," and § 35-13-205(a)(iv) expressly defines that to include an animal that "provides emotional support." Survives the HUD withdrawal. **Qualifier:** § 35-13-201(c) permits the animal "in accordance with the federal Fair Housing Act," so mechanics are federally tethered — weaker than CO's CADA, and no WY case law construes it. | **KS RESOLVED 2026-08-29 (see KS re-audit rows below). NE remains the live gap** — still tagged on the `NEEDS_REVIEW` generic clause and unchecked. Use the four-way classification, not the original three-way. |
| **Does the state's misrepresentation-penalty statute reach HOUSING?** | **Yes for WY.** § 35-13-203(b) penalizes misrepresenting a service *or assistance* animal to obtain rights "set forth in this article," and § 35-13-201(c) — the residential-leasing right — is in that article. **Contrast MN**, where § 609.833 likely does *not* reach housing. | **Yes.** A penalty statute sitting in a public-accommodations chapter may not reach a lease at all. Don't assume scope from the fact that a penalty exists. |
| **Attorney-fee reciprocity — is mutual language required or voluntary?** | **No WY reciprocity statute.** WY follows the American Rule; a contract must "unequivocally provide" for fees. WY is not among the seven reciprocity states (CA, FL, HI, MT, OR, UT, WA). A landlord-only clause would be **enforceable** in WY. | **Yes, and it exposed a §5a.1 violation.** The prevailing-party language in `default-by-tenant` was **forced by Colorado law** (C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(II)) and inherited by WY/MN/ND/SD **unclassified** — the exact failure §5a.1 exists to prevent. WY's kept it as a deliberate giveaway. **MN, ND, and SD remain unclassified.** |
| **Deposit "use" vs "return" as separate clauses** | WY had both folded into one clause; split to the CO pattern. Two deliberate giveaways logged: the generic allows cleaning only if "substantially less clean," vs. § 1-21-1208(a)'s "clean to the condition at start"; and 1208(a)'s catch-all "any other costs this Lease provides for" is not carried over. | Yes — where a state's deposit clause is combined, check whether splitting loses statutory latitude, and log any giveaway as a decision rather than drift. |
| **Source reliability does not transfer between states** | Hemlane produced **four** distinct fabricated WY claims in one session (a 2023 interest-bearing-account mandate, a deposit cap, a 75% interest-payment rule, new DV deposit provisions) — one contradicted by a different paragraph on its own page. LeaseWisely published ~15 fabricated "required WY disclosures" with no citations. | **Yes.** A domain that was accurate for one state is not thereby reliable for another. Re-test per state. |

- **Shared-clause propagation owed from the CO re-audit (2026-08-27).** Two multi-state clauses were edited during CO's re-audit and owe notes in the other tagged states' logs, per the new rule (CO log §5a.1): `lead-based-paint` (CO;WY;KS;NE;MN — Lead Warning Statement corrected to verbatim; **uniform federal fix, all five inherit it safely**) and `assistance-animal-accommodation` (KS;NE — moved to NEEDS_REVIEW). Neither is a content problem for those states; both are bookkeeping obligations. **WY's is discharged (WY log §Addendum 2026-08-28, items 1–2): lead-paint classified UNIFORM and inherited; the assistance-animal row does not reach WY, which carries its own override. KS and NE remain outstanding.**
- **KS and NE are carrying a flagged assistance-animal clause.** The generic `assistance-animal-accommodation` (federal baseline only) is tagged KS;NE and is now NEEDS_REVIEW because the federal ESA picture is unsettled. Neither state has been checked for an independent state-law basis the way CO was (CADA). **This is a live substantive gap in two states currently marked complete** — a one-question audit each: does the state have its own disability-accommodation statute reaching assistance animals? Worth queuing rather than carrying forward.
- **The remaining completed states were verified at default settings (Sonnet/medium/plain search).** **WY has now been re-audited (2026-08-28) and it found two real errors** — a fabricated statute citation in shipped lease text (`§ 35-13-207`) and an unclassified state-driven shared-clause edit. Two for two: both re-audited states surfaced errors that had shipped as `VERIFIED`. KS, NE, MN, ND, and SD remain untested. Original entry: CO's re-audit at higher settings found three hard errors that had shipped as VERIFIED — a carpet lookback taken from a superseded bill draft (5 years vs. the enrolled 10), a documentation window stated as 120 days against a statutory 60, and a clause citing the notice-to-quit statute for a returned-check rule while asserting a "$20 statutory cap" that exists in no statute. WY, KS, NE, MN, ND, and SD were all built under the same conditions that produced those errors. Not a claim any of them is wrong — a claim that none has been tested. WY is queued first.
- **Immigration-status inquiry prohibition** and **right to call police (non-waivable)** — both CO standing rules, confirmed absent for Kansas, Nebraska, and now North Dakota. **Still genuinely open for Wyoming** — the WY re-audit did not close these; they remain unchecked there.
- **Rental application/tenant screening fairness act analog** — CO-originated, confirmed absent for WY and now ND (solid evidence for both); still not found for KS or NE. Genuinely lower research confidence for KS/NE than the WY/ND findings — worth a dedicated research pass for those two rather than continuing to carry them forward unresolved.
- **Immigrant tenant protection act analog** — resolved as confirmed-absent for NE and now ND (both folding into the immigration-status-inquiry finding); still not checked for WY or KS specifically.
- **Nebraska's own named-topic canvass** — only pass 1 has been run as of this file's last update (session 2 of the NE log). Pass 2 is still outstanding — don't treat any NE row above as final until that second pass confirms it.
- **Minnesota (state #5) was never folded into this checklist file** — a gap in the base file itself, discovered during North Dakota's session. MN's decision log has its own extensive findings that should be retroactively added as a column here; ND's own canvass this session was run against CO/WY/KS/NE only, not cross-checked against MN's findings. Whoever revisits this file next should add MN's column before (or alongside) any further state's work, to close this gap.
- **Fee-shifting-mutuality question — RESOLVED for WY (2026-08-28):** no WY reciprocity statute; a landlord-only clause would be enforceable, so the mutual language in `default-by-tenant` is a voluntary giveaway, kept by decision. **The CO-driven edit remains unclassified for MN, ND, and SD.** Original entry: CO/KS/NE/MN all have an open question about whether their `default-by-tenant`-family fee-shifting language is genuinely mutual. **Resolved for ND specifically** (§47-16-13.6 confirmed mutual, "prevailing party" language matches the generic clause exactly) — but the broader cross-state consolidation, checking whether CO/WY/KS/NE/MN's own versions are internally consistent with each other, has still not been done as a single pass.
- **North Dakota's Chapter 47-32 (the eviction chapter) was never independently read from primary source** — everything ND-related about eviction notice mechanics, cure rights, and the specific eviction grounds comes from secondary sources or partial citations. This is the one meaningful primary-source gap remaining in ND's otherwise-thorough verification; worth closing if Taylor can supply the chapter text the way Chapter 47-16's text was supplied directly this session.
- **Last-month's-rent deposit-application restriction for ND** — genuinely inconclusive on the evidence available. One weak, uncited secondary source suggests a KS-shaped rule; the actual deposit statute (§47-16-07.1) doesn't address it directly. Worth a dedicated primary-source check if Chapter 47-32 or other ND materials become available.

Code Ann. § 66-28-201(d)) - `late-fee-limit-tn`; **no cap in other counties** - `late-fee-tn-other`, `edu-late-fee-rules-tn`. VA (2026-09-28): **Present**: late charge only if in a written lease, capped at the lesser of 10% of periodic rent or 10% of the remaining balance (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204(E)) - `late-fee-limit-va`. AL (2026-09-28): **Confirmed absent (statutes)** - `edu-no-late-fee-cap-al` PA (2026-09-29): **Confirmed absent (statutes)** - search 5 - `edu-no-late-fee-cap-pa` |
| **Statutory order of applying a tenant's payment** | ND | **Confirmed absent** — no ND rule either way; **2025 SB 2235** ("rents and the priority of payments under a rental agreement") not enacted. Rent-first ordering in `application-of-payments` is a contract choice in ND, not statutorily compelled | Yes GA (2026-09-28): Not located. SC (2026-09-28): Not located - no statutory order; late charges are rent (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-210(11)); `application-of-payments` tagged. TN (2026-09-28): Not located - no statutory order of application; 'rent' includes all payments under the lease (Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-104(13)); `application-of-payments` tagged. ## Instructions for the next state

> **RETIRED 2026-09-29: superseded by `lease-clause-sop.md`.** Follow the SOP, not this list. These instructions are kept only as history, because the SOP and the state logs cite them by number. Nothing new is added here.

1. Copy this table (or work directly from it).
2. For every row, produce Present / Confirmed Absent with a primary-source citation, or explicitly write "Not Yet Checked" if a first pass doesn't get to it — never leave a row silently blank.
3. **Superseded by instruction 22.** One pass at the correct settings is the right number. The only second look is at rows written from recall rather than with the section open.
4. Add any new topics the state's own core-landlord-tenant-statute reading surfaces as new rows in the correct section above (or a new section, if it doesn't fit an existing one) — the next state after this one needs to see it too. Nebraska added four; North Dakota added five (see "New topics added by North Dakota" section above): double-letting-of-a-room prohibition, direct contractual termination rights outside the eviction process, fraudulent-misrepresentation termination right, the payment-method-fee ban, and eviction-record sealing.
5. Update this file's per-state columns and hand it forward.
6. **Watch for overconfident secondary sources.** This project has now hit the same pattern repeatedly and independently — Wyoming (Hemlane), Kansas (a fabricated statute citation), Nebraska twice, and North Dakota twice more: multiple landlord-industry guides citing N.D.C.C. § 14-02.5-07 for a "must accept Section 8 vouchers" rule when the actual operative section was § 14-02.5-02 (§14-02.5-07 is titled "Residential real estate-related transaction," an unrelated provision); and a claim that ordinary ND lease violations get a statutory cure opportunity, which turned out to be unsupported once checked against the same site's own separate eviction-process page. Treat any specific number, penalty, or citation from a non-primary source as unverified until checked against the actual statute text, regardless of how confidently it's stated or how many sources repeat it.
7. **Check adjacent chapters, not just the core act.** Nebraska's smoke-detector and CO-alarm duties, and its bad-check restitution statute, all live outside Chapter 76. North Dakota's smoke-detector duty (§23-13-15, Title 23 Health and Safety), its self-help-eviction damages measure (§32-03-29, Title 32), its bad-check fee cap (§6-08-16, Title 6 Banking), and its housing-discrimination protections (§§14-02.4, 14-02.5, Title 14) all live outside Chapter 47-16 too — the same pattern, now confirmed a fourth and fifth time. A first pass confined to the core act's table of contents will reliably miss real findings.
8. **When a live participant (the person you're working with) can supply primary-source text directly, take it seriously and re-verify against it immediately.** North Dakota's session was substantially strengthened by Taylor providing the complete Chapter 47-16 text directly partway through, plus the enacted text of two specific sections (§47-16-20.1, §32-03-29) that had been stuck as blocked or weak-evidence items for the entire rest of the session. This isn't a substitute for independent verification, but it's a legitimate and often faster path to primary-source confidence than continued guessing at search queries — don't be too proud of the search-only approach to pass up a direct text contribution when it's offered.
9. **Propagate any edit to a shared clause.** If you change the `bodyText`, `rule_type`, or `content_type` of a clause tagged with more than one state, you must: write a note in *every* tagged state's log, reset `last_checked` for the row, and record whether the change is **uniform** (federal law or generic mechanics — safe for all tagged states to inherit) or **state-driven** (one state's law forced it, in which case the others may need their own override rather than the edited text). A state-driven edit inherited silently is how a clause becomes wrong for five states in order to be right for one. Programmatic check before committing: list every row where `states` holds more than one state and `last_checked` post-dates the earliest tagged state's completion — each hit needs a log note or a written reason none is required.
10. **Ask for primary text after two failed searches, not after two failed sessions.** Instruction 8 above already says to take direct text when it's offered; this adds the trigger. When a specific controlling section has been identified and two search attempts haven't produced its actual text — or have produced conflicting versions — ask for it directly rather than searching a third time or shipping the item at NEEDS_REVIEW. On CO this shortcut worked twice, and the second time the primary text turned up five findings beyond the question that prompted it. Corollary: never mark an item VERIFIED on secondary summaries alone when the controlling section was identified but never actually read — NEEDS_REVIEW is fine, VERIFIED is not.

11. **Run the citation-existence screen — against `notes` as well as `bodyText`.** Extract every statutory citation and confirm the cited section exists. Tier the results: citations inside `LEASE_CLAUSE` rows are what tenants actually read and must be verified first; `LANDLORD_EDUCATION` citations are lower stakes. Two cautions learned the hard way: (a) match the spelled-out `C.R.S. section 38-12-1301` form and continuation cites like `sections 18-13-107.3 and 18-13-107.7`, not just the `§` glyph — an early version of this screen undercounted by ~20% and the miss fell almost entirely on one state's drafting convention; (b) the screen cannot catch a valid citation that is *described* wrongly, so it supplements reading the statute, never replaces it.

12. **Notes are a propagation vector — screen them.** Across the library, **161 citations appear only in `notes` and have never been screened**, of which ~138 are asserted plainly as support rather than framed as corrections. Notes are where the next state's research starts: a phantom cite in a note reads as a prior finding and travels. This already happened — WY's dead `§ 35-13-207` propagated into `edu-service-animal-fraud-ks`'s notes as a "parallel finding" and would have reached the next state after that. The unscreened pool is concentrated: **NE 44, ND 27, SD 27, WY 13, KS 12, MN 11, CO 1.** Carve out citations explicitly framed as corrected/repealed/unconfirmed — key the carve-out off that language automatically rather than maintaining a manual flag list.

13. **Confirm the CSV version before doing any work.** Both the CO and WY re-audits ran on a CSV that predated South Dakota (361 rows, zero SD content) and each produced a branch off the wrong trunk; reconciling them cost a full session. At session start, check the row count and state-tag counts against what the project's records say. As of 2026-08-28 the canonical file is **`steinoak_clauses_updated_57.csv` — 395 rows; CO 106, WY 96, NE 95, KS 93, MN 70, SD 37, ND 33.** Only one chat should write a given version number.

14. **Delimit any new state's addition to a shared clause's `notes` clearly (e.g. lead with the state code), not blended into the existing run-on paragraph.** Every citation-extraction pass since Wyoming has had to reverse-engineer per-state boundaries out of undelimited prose covering all seven states' research history in one field — a consistent convention removes this entire class of risk for whoever extracts citations from this state's work later.

15. **Record the evidentiary basis of every Confirmed Absent finding: full primary-text read of the relevant chapter/title, or secondary-source agreement only.** This is exactly what later determines whether a finding becomes `CITED` (full-text-verified absence) or `CONFIRMED_ABSENT` (secondary-source-only) in the per-state citations file — recording it at research time avoids re-inferring evidentiary strength from prose tone afterward. North Dakota's pass did this well by construction (full-chapter reads throughout) and shipped zero `CONFIRMED_ABSENT` rows as a direct result.

16. **Flag any citation that isn't a plain state-code section the moment it's found** — administrative-code rules, case law, federal CFR/statute. These need different downstream monitoring treatment (agency rulemaking isn't visible to a legislative bill-tracking search at all, regardless of state), a pattern already true for KS's K.A.R., ND's N.D. Admin. Code, SD's ARSD, and NE's frozen-date CFR citation.

17. **Don't cite a bill as authority without confirming it was actually enacted, not just introduced or passed one chamber.** This project has independently hit "an introduced/failed draft mistaken for law" at least three times: Colorado's carpet-lookback figure (sourced from a superseded introduced draft), North Dakota's SB 2222 (assumed enacted; it failed on second reading in the Senate), and Kansas's HB 2357.

18. **Don't import another state's statutory architecture (an eviction-grounds list, a notice-and-cure structure, etc.) as a starting hypothesis without independently verifying each element against the new state's own primary text.** North Dakota's citation-extraction pass had to correct a wholesale-imported Kansas/Nebraska eviction-grounds list that turned out not to exist anywhere in North Dakota law at all.

19. **When this checklist or a decision log claims a topic "Present, already covered," confirm an actual CSV row exists for it before moving on — don't trust the claim itself.** This exact gap (asserted covered, no row ever built) has happened twice now: Minnesota's domestic-violence lease-termination statute and North Dakota's own DV-release statute. It's worse than an honest absence, since the false "already covered" note stops any future canvass from ever re-flagging it.

20. **If a state's pass is deliberately scoped state-level-only (as agreed for Ohio, state #8), flag any municipal ordinance found but don't resolve it, and don't let it bleed into state-level clause text as if it applied everywhere.** Matches the existing "noted, not resolved" treatment already given to Denver/Boulder (Colorado) and Minneapolis/St. Paul (Minnesota).

21. **Re-verify any pre-existing clause already in the library for the new state before assuming it's correct just because it shipped** — e.g. Ohio's `security-deposit-interest-oh` (moved to `edu-security-deposit-interest-oh` by the 2026-09-29 scrub), untouched by any verification pass to date. Every one of the 7 states re-audited so far turned up at least one error in content that had shipped `VERIFIED`.

22. **No re-audits. The two passes run for CO, WY, KS, NE, MN, ND and SD were a one-time SETTINGS difference, not a repetition requirement, and no completed state will be audited again** (see the standing rule at the top of this file). For states #1–#7, pass 1 was run at Claude default settings (Sonnet, medium effort, research off) and pass 2 at the corrected settings (Opus, high effort, research available on request). Pass 2 therefore found something every time because the *settings* changed, not because re-reading the same material is inherently productive. Ohio (state #8) was run at the corrected settings from the start, so **one audit is the correct number**; "the re-audit has found something in 8 consecutive states" is a confound, and citing it as a reason to re-run a correctly-settinged state is bad inference. What *does* reliably need a second look is narrower and unrelated to settings: **any row written from recall of a chapter read earlier in the session rather than with the specific section open.** In Ohio's own single pass that subset produced four corrections (a landlord-facing criminal penalty missed entirely, an "aligned" verdict that was backwards, a missing statutory forfeiture, and a vague carve-out that has a hard numeric threshold). Track which rows were written section-open vs. recall-reconstructed, and verify only the latter.

23. **When a research question is actually about how the app itself behaves — not what the law says — ask Claude Code to check by executing the real code, rather than reasoning about it from written documentation (including this project's own CLAUDE.md and decision logs, which can themselves be wrong).** Mid-way through Ohio's canvass, a library-integrity question surfaced (does a blank `states` field on `security-deposit-return` actually suppress the clause, and does `supersedes` actually do anything) that both this checklist's own prior entries and CLAUDE.md's Known Issues had already answered — wrongly, in the more dangerous direction, for over three weeks. The mistake was never caught by re-reading prose about the code; it was caught the one time someone actually ran the filter logic against real shipped data. A question with a definite, checkable mechanical answer should be checked, not inferred — ask Claude Code directly when a research session hits one.

24. **Before relying on the "screen the shared multi-state base rows" step to catch every gap, separately check every `REQUIRED` clause *family* (a base clause plus all its per-state overrides) for whether the new state has any coverage at all.** That screening step only looks at base rows tagged to 2+ states — a base clause already superseded down to one or zero remaining generic-tag states (because every other state that reached it wrote its own override) is invisible to it by construction, which is exactly backwards: those are the clauses a new state is *most* likely to also need its own override for, since it means the clause's substance reliably varies state to state. Ohio's own research fully confirmed the assistance-animal-accommodation fee ban applied (OAC 4112-5-07(C)) but never produced a CSV row for it, because `assistance-animal-accommodation`'s base row is tagged only `KS` (CO/WY/NE/MN/ND/SD all superseded it) and so never appeared as a "2+ state" row to extend. As of Ohio (state #8), exactly two `REQUIRED` clause families are in this blind spot and need an explicit manual check for every future state: `assistance-animal-accommodation` (base row tagged `KS` only) and `security-deposit-return` (base row blank, all 8 states superseded). **Amended 2026-09-29 (instruction 66):** for `security-deposit-return`, the check is that the state's deposit-return rules are covered, as a lease clause or as education; no statute recorded in the library requires the lease to restate them.


25. **When you don't know exactly which section you need, ask for a range — the whole article or chapter — not one section at a time.** Added after California (state #9), where several rounds went: ask Taylor for §X, Taylor supplies it, "that's not the right one," ask for §X+1, repeat — until Taylor just supplied the entire article, which resolved it immediately. Instruction 10 says *when* to ask for primary text; this says *how much*: if you're confident of the exact section, ask for it; if you're only confident of the neighborhood, ask for the neighborhood up front. One oversized paste is far cheaper than five round trips.

26. **Prior vetted states are a guide, not gold standard — they are not immutable, and the default is to REUSE and EXTEND existing clauses, not write new state-specific ones.** California's pass treated the eight earlier states as untouchable "core states," wrote every CA clause as a new CA-only row, and never tagged a single existing clause `CA` until Taylor prompted it at the very end (log §§5.32–5.38) — a CA lease built from that CSV would have had no severability, notices, governing-law or maintenance clauses at all. Run these two steps **in this order, as the first half of the pass, before drafting any new state-specific rows**:
    1. **Tag first.** Screen *every* active clause from the vetted states (CO, WY, KS, NE, MN, ND, SD, OH, CA, …) — not only the base rows shared by 2+ states (instruction 24 already covers one blind spot of that narrower screen; this closes the rest). Exclude only the dormant, never-vetted rows from non-project states. For each: does it apply to the new state as written? If yes, add the state tag (read the full text first — never tag on title; CA §5.33). If it *almost* applies, note it for step 2.
    2. **Then, for every new clause you're about to write, check it against the existing library first.** Is it genuinely unique to this state, or does it overlap an existing clause? Look for close matches, not just exact ones (`topic_key` in `lease-clauses.csv` now makes this a group-by — use it). An existing clause that's close can often be **massaged to cover the new state alongside its current states** (a self-limiting "except as permitted by applicable law," a carve-out that's true everywhere) — that's preferable to a near-duplicate new row, because one row is one thing to maintain and re-verify. Editing another state's row is allowed; follow instruction 9 (propagate the note, record uniform vs. state-driven, reset `last_checked`). Also re-check any new row against the others you've just written for the same state.
    **Priority, stated plainly:** correctly covering the new state's statutes is paramount. Consolidation is a strong nice-to-have — never merge or generalize a clause if it would weaken or blur a real state divergence (e.g. CO can require written repair notice and CA cannot; those stay separate, CA §5.36). When in doubt, a separate row that's right beats a shared row that's approximately right.
27. **Every active row must carry its own `verification_status` in `lease-clauses.csv` — a blank status is an error, not a convention.** Added 2026-09-25 at the Nevada sync. Colorado's 63 CO-only rows used to have blank status because on 2026-09-13 that data was moved into `lease-clause-citations-CO.csv`. A session holding only the CSV read those rows as unverified, and Nevada's pass spent real effort working around them. The data has been copied back, so all active rows now carry a status. The per-state `lease-clause-citations-<STATE>.csv` files still exist and stay in sync, but the CSV is the canonical copy. If you find a blank status, flag it; don't treat it as meaning "see another file."
28. **Screen every clause for typography- or placement-conditioned effect, and treat an absent formatting attribute as a product gap, not a drafting nicety.** Added after Texas (state #11), where 17 lease terms are void or ineffective unless underlined or bold (one underline-*only*, §92.162(b); one a prescribed heading, §92.0131(c)). Search each new state's code for "underlined", "boldface", "conspicuous", "separate document" and "substantially equivalent", and record every hit in the state log's layout table. Also screen for **omission sanctions that forfeit money** rather than void a term (Texas: leaving out the early-termination statement releases all delinquent rent).
29. **Read primary text from the official legislative site, and ask whether a special session has met since the last regular one.** Added after Texas: its 2025 called sessions amended the Property Code (§24.0043, H.B. 16, 2nd C.S.), and a host compilation labelled "2025" gave no sign of it. History lines on the official page are the only reliable currency evidence.
30. **List the state's opt-in landlord rights explicitly (ref 694.1).** A right that exists only if the lease invokes it is silently forfeited by a lease that doesn't. Texas has more than fifteen. Offer each as a CONDITIONAL row, or record why not.
31. **Screen every shared clause for 'end of term ends possession' wording in any state with just-cause eviction or good-cause renewal.** Added after New Jersey: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.3(a) makes expiration no ground to end a covered tenancy, which broke `surrender-end-of-term` and `holdover`.
32. **Check whether a statute requires specific text inside any shared fee-shifting, deposit or other clause the state is tagged on.** Added after New Jersey: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.67 forces a bold sentence into any lease attorney-fee clause, so `default-by-tenant` could not be tagged as written. Same shape as TX's Occ. Code §2308.253(e) (TX1.22).
33. **Screen every shared clause that promises a cure period for 'any other' breach against the state's no-cure termination grounds.** Added after Florida: `default-by-tenant` makes every non-rent breach curable after notice, which would contractually give up Fla. Stat. §83.56(2)(a)'s 7-day no-cure termination (intentional damage, fraudulent entry, repeated disturbance). A generous shared clause can forfeit a landlord right as silently as a ceiling-only figure (K.3).
34. **Read the session law's effective-date clause for every recent amendment, even when the official compilation already prints it.** Added after Florida: the 2026 Florida Statutes show §83.56(2)(a) as amended by ch. 2026-143, but that law takes effect 2026-10-01. A current-looking official page can print law that is not yet in force; rows must state the date.
35. **When the official compilation prints no history lines, establish currency from the session laws and record which sections' currency is unconfirmed.** Added after Arizona: azleg.gov ARS pages have no source or history line, and the compilation reflects law effective January 1 after the latest session. That cuts both ways: a section can print an amendment whose effective date has not arrived, and a section that is IN FORCE NOW but self-repeals before that January 1 is simply MISSING (Arizona §33-1332, Laws 2023 ch. 204, in force to 2026-12-31, absent from the section index). A 'full read' of the compilation is therefore not a full read of current law. Confirm each recent amendment by Laws chapter and effective date (instruction 34), check recent session laws for delayed repeals, and when that is not possible say so in the row's notes rather than implying the text's date.
36. **A state is not done until four gap-discovery sources have run, and the log's completion table says so for each: (1) the statute walk (the core landlord-tenant chapter, read whole); (2) a real-lease comparison; (3) a landlord-scenario screen; (4) a search for law outside the landlord-tenant title (proof-of-absence and cross-title searches).** Set by Taylor, 2026-09-27, after Arizona. For source (2), find a real, professional lease for the state yourself: the state Realtors association's residential lease (or a copy a brokerage or property manager posts), a lease published by a state agency or public body, or one a real property-management company posts. Generic multi-state form sites (ezLandlordForms, LawDistrict, PandaDoc, Rocket Lawyer, eForms and the like) don't qualify. If nothing qualifies, name the best paid attorney-reviewed product and its price and ask Taylor whether to buy it; never settle for a template. Record the lease's URL, publisher and edition, and why it qualifies. Map its provisions by topic against the state's library, as a lead only (instruction 6), and record: missing required clauses, corrections, new rows and confirmed absences. Don't reproduce copyrighted text. For source (3), **generate the scenarios yourself; never ask Taylor for his experience.** List the everyday situations a landlord in the state meets, from application through move-out, sale and foreclosure (AZ log §18.1's 59-scenario map is the model; reuse it and add anything state-specific). Run each against the state's active library, and where no row answers it, search the statutes and read any hit section-open. Taylor's own experience is Colorado-only and is already in the CO research, so it is not an input for any other state. In Arizona this screen found two real gaps (towing, selling a rented property). **Enforced, not just stated:** every state log must carry a table with one row per source, labelled exactly "Gap-discovery source 1 — statute walk", "Gap-discovery source 2 — real-lease comparison", "Gap-discovery source 3 — landlord-scenario screen" and "Gap-discovery source 4 — outside-title search". Each row must say Done and cite the log section (§...). Claude Code runs `scripts/clause-library/check-gap-discovery.py` at every sync, and a state is not done while it fails. "Partial", "not applicable" and "pending" fail. **Backfill (audited 2026-09-27 against every log), a one-time targeted pass per state (a scalpel, not a re-audit):** the scenario screen for all twelve states other than CO and AZ; a real-lease comparison for MN, OH, CA, NV, TX, NJ and FL (never run) and for WY and ND (run only against free templates); and the outside-title search finished for NE, MN, OH, CA and NV, where topics are still "Not located" rather than confirmed absent statute-wide. **Completed 2026-09-27/28:** all twelve states ran their missing sources, their log sections were appended, and `check-gap-discovery.py --all` passes for all 14 states. Cell changes were applied in place; topics with no existing row are in "New topics added by the gap-discovery backfill".
37. **The statute walk (source 1) isn't finished until the core act's citation inventory is diffed against the library.** Pull the core landlord-tenant chapter's full section-number-and-title index from the official site, and list every section cited in no active row's `bodyText` or `notes`. That list is a gap list. Run the same check one level down for any section the library cites but renders only in part: a subsection can be missing from an already-cited section. Kansas's backfill found five uncited sections of its own act this way, and Nebraska's found five, including the fire/casualty section. Added 2026-09-28 (KS, NE backfill; Taylor approved).
38. **A claim of coverage must point at a real row, and it must stay true.** Whenever the checklist gains rows or cells for a completed state, re-check that every clause id it names exists. Claude Code runs `scripts/clause-library/check-checklist-reconciliation.py` at every sync, and it fails on a named id that isn't in the CSV. The same applies to claims inside the CSV's own `notes` ("already covered", "already reflected elsewhere", "covered by"): confirm a row exists for each. North Dakota's backfill found two cells asserting coverage with no row behind them, and Minnesota's found a `notes` claim with no row. Added 2026-09-28 (ND, MN backfill; Taylor approved).
39. **Proof-of-absence searches use the statute's own words, every word form, and a control term.** Search the colloquial term and the statute's term of art: "smoke-sensitive alarm device" (NJ), "smoke alarm" rather than "smoke detector" (MN), "clandestine lab site" (MN), "clandestine" rather than "methamphetamine laboratory" (NE). Search every word form ("renter's" vs "renters"). Before certifying any absence, run a nonsense control term to confirm the engine reports true empties, and record how the engine matches (exact phrase vs loose keywords). Nebraska's engine is loose, so the method that works in Arizona manufactures false absences there. A keyword probe is a screen, never a verdict. Added 2026-09-28 (NJ, MN, NE backfill; Taylor approved).
40. **Currency checks read the section's history, not just its text.** Read the revisor's recent-history block and the full History line (a sidebar can hide that an amendment came from a special session). Never strip a session law's amendment markers: they are the only evidence of what is actually new. When a core section shows as repealed, read the repealing act's other sections, because the duty has usually moved, not disappeared. A codified page can silently serve pre-amendment law, so cite the session law for anything recent. Added 2026-09-28 (MN backfill; Taylor approved).
41. **A real lease qualifies on provenance and on content, and the two can come apart.** A state agency's own lease satisfies the publisher test and can still be a relabelled multi-state template. Look for the state's name find-and-replaced into ordinary sentences, and for deduction lists or cure periods lifted from another state. Record the edition date, and treat every divergence as a question for primary text. A public housing authority's lease is shaped by 24 CFR 966.4, so it is a lead only. A public university's housing contract is unusable where the act excludes educational institutions (Ohio R.C. 5321.01(C)). The state Realtors form is not always reachable; an apartment-association lease also qualifies. Added 2026-09-28 (OH backfill; Taylor approved).
42. **Titles and consolidations mislead.** A section's title can point away from its content: K.S.A. 58-2549 is titled "Receipt of rent" and is an anti-waiver rule. So open the section; a title search is not a canvass. When one row covers several subdivisions of a statute, check it subdivision by subdivision. Ohio's §5321.13 coverage was right for (A), (C), (E) and (F) and missed (B) and (D). Added 2026-09-28 (KS, OH backfill; Taylor approved).
43. **Each state keeps one Claude Desktop chat, reused for every circle-back, and each circle-back starts by clearing that chat's leftovers.** Taylor's call (2026-09-28): a new chat per circle-back would multiply chats and make it unclear which one is current. The cost of reuse is that a long chat accumulates old files in `/mnt/user-data/outputs/` (the ND chat held ~40 old `steinoak_clauses_updated_NNN.csv` copies and an old log at the backfill) and remembers row counts and decisions that have since changed. So before any work in a reopened state chat: (1) delete every old CSV, decision log and checklist copy from the outputs folder, and say what was deleted; (2) take the files Taylor uploads for this task as the only source of truth, and run instruction 13's version check against them; (3) where anything earlier in the chat conflicts with the uploaded files, the uploaded files win, and say so rather than silently mixing the two. Name every output file for the task it belongs to (for example `lease-clauses-ND-delta.csv`), never a bare version number that an old copy could share. Added 2026-09-28.
44. **Screen shared clauses for terms a statute converts into landlord duties by incorporation.** Added after Georgia: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50(d) requires the demand for possession and the 3-day notice to be posted on the door AND 'delivered via any additional method or methods agreed upon in the rental agreement'. A lease that generously adds e-mail or text delivery thereby makes those methods mandatory for the landlord's eviction notices, and a missed method can defeat the notice. `notices` is safe only because it designates no alternative method. Same family as instruction 33 (a generous clause forfeiting a right) and K.3 (self-limiting text hides the problem): read each state's notice and procedure statutes for phrases such as 'agreed upon in the rental agreement', 'as provided in the lease' or 'if the lease so provides', and check what the shared clauses say on that point. Added 2026-09-28 (GA).
45. **A host copy's history line beats a fetch-tool summary, and a summary can be stale.** Added after Georgia: WebFetch served the pre-2026 text of O.C.G.A. § 44-1-16 (and a summary of § 44-7-50 with no text) while the same Justia URL, read in the browser, printed the version effective 2026-07-01 with its history line and amendment note. The fetch tool also refused verbatim reproduction twice. Where a browser is available, read the page itself and quote the history line; treat a fetch-tool summary as a lead, and never as currency evidence (instructions 29, 40). Added 2026-09-28 (GA).
46. **When a subdivision of the official compilation reads oddly, read every session law in its history line before relying on it.** Added after North Carolina: S.L. 2025-52, s. 3 and S.L. 2025-54, s. 12.4 both rewrote N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-46(i)(3) and moved the frivolous-appeal fee rule into a new (i)(4), each retroactive to 2024-09-09; the official compilation merged them into a garbled '(4) court and the landlord is the prevailing party, delay.' followed by a '(5)' carrying the superseded sentence. Two acts amending the same subsection in one session is the warning sign. Cite the session law for the current text and record the glitch in the row's notes (instructions 34, 40). Added 2026-09-28 (NC).
47. **Check the state's electronic-transactions act for exclusions before accepting any electronic notice method.** Added after North Carolina: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 66-313(e)(2) says the UETA does not apply to 'any notice of default ... or eviction, or the right to cure, under ... a rental agreement for a primary residence'. A lease clause or real-lease form (the NC REALTORS lease allows e-mail and text notices) that makes e-mail a notice method for those notices would rest on nothing. Search each state's UETA scope section for 'eviction', 'rental agreement' and 'primary residence', and screen `notices`, `electronic-signatures` and any electronic-notice addendum against it. Same family as instruction 44. Added 2026-09-28 (NC).
48. **When a statute lets the lease itself serve as a required notice, offer the clause and reconcile every shared clause that promises a separate notice.** Added after South Carolina: S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-710(B) makes a lease paragraph in the statutory words ("IF YOU DO NOT PAY YOUR RENT ON TIME ...") the written nonpayment notice for the whole tenancy, and S.C. Code Ann. § 27-37-10(B) requires it in bold conspicuous type. The shared `default-by-tenant` makes nonpayment a default only after the tenant 'receiv[es] written notice from Landlord', which, read against the landlord, can require a second notice and undo the shortcut. `nonpayment-notice-sc` states that it is that notice. Search each state's notice statutes for 'contained in the rental agreement', 'in the lease' and 'substantially equivalent provision'; record the formatting as an Addendum M.12 gap. The reverse of instruction 44 (a lease term creating a notice duty) and the same family as instruction 33. Added 2026-09-28 (SC).
49. **Where the state penalizes knowingly using a prohibited lease term, a savings sentence does not make a void term safe to tag.** Added after South Carolina: S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-330(b) gives the tenant actual damages plus up to the deposit and fees (up to three months' rent if malicious) when a landlord deliberately uses a lease containing terms it knows are prohibited. The shared `early-termination` states a 10-day cure against a 14-day statutory right; its 'Nothing in this Section limits any right ... under applicable law' would keep the right but not the penalty exposure. Tag a shared clause only if its text is lawful as written; otherwise use a variant (`early-termination-ks`) or an override. Check for a URLTA § 1.403-style penalty in every state (AZ1.4 found none in Arizona). Added 2026-09-28 (SC).
50. **Read the official compilation's own currency statement before relying on it, and screen every act of the sessions it does not cover in full text.** Added after South Carolina: scstatehouse.gov states its Code is 'current through the 2025 Session', and three 2026 acts that change landlord-tenant law (DV termination, unlawful-occupant removal and appeal stays, eviction-record removal) appear nowhere in it. The Legislature's act list gave every 2026 act number; each act's full text was searched for the chapter's section prefix and landlord-tenant terms. Cite the act for anything not yet codified. Extends instructions 29, 35 and 40. Added 2026-09-28 (SC).
51. **Where the landlord-tenant act applies only in some counties or cities, build two versions only where the lease wording must differ, and mark every row's scope.** Added after Tennessee (the county-layer pilot; Taylor, 2026-09-28): the URLTA covers 17 of 95 counties, and the other 78 use a thin general chapter. Pairs share the topic_key, a choice_group prefixed `<st>-<act>-` (TN: `tn-urlta-*`), the act-county variant is `is_default` TRUE, and both supersede the shared base; rules that apply everywhere stay single rows. Every row's notes open with a scope marker (`TN-SCOPE: ACT COUNTIES ONLY` / `NON-ACT COUNTIES ONLY` / `STATEWIDE` / `BOTH REGIMES`) and carry the pilot note, so the future county layer can find them. Record the county list in an education row, and flag the product need for a property-county attribute (Addendum M). Screen checklist cells the same way: say which counties an answer covers.
52. **Population-bracket and frozen-census statutes name places without naming them; derive the list from primary census data and record how.** Added after Tennessee: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-102(a) covers counties 'having a population of more than seventy-five thousand (75,000), according to the 2010 federal census', and 2021 Pub. Ch. 182 § 2 deleted 'or any subsequent federal census', freezing the list. Record the census year, whether and by which act it is frozen, the file used (TN: Census Bureau co-est2019-alldata, CENSUS2010POP), and the counts on each side of the line (TN: Anderson 75,129 in; Putnam 72,321 out). Other bracket statutes (rental inspection districts, condo conversion 'Class 1 and 2' counties, Davidson registration) get the same treatment or an open item.
53. **When the same rule is enacted twice, in the general chapter and the act chapter, read and cite both, and compare them subsection by subsection.** Added after Tennessee: DV termination (Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 66-28-205, 66-7-112), assistance animals (§§ 66-28-406, 66-7-111), DV eviction limits (§§ 66-28-517(g), 66-7-109(e)) and firearms from 2027 (§§ 66-28-206, 66-7-113) each appear in both chapters so they reach every county. A search that stops at the act chapter will call a statewide rule county-limited. Extends instruction 51.
54. **When a state's act tiers duties by how many units the landlord owns, pair the clause only where the lease wording must differ, make the variant that is lawful for every landlord the default, and mark every row's scope.** Added after Virginia: Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204(J)(2) (landlords of 4 or fewer units need not take cards), § 55.1-1250 (they may limit redemption to once per lease period), § 55.1-1204(K) (renewal and rent-increase notice only for more than 4 units) and § 55.1-1212.1 (plug-in solar from 2027-01-01) produced four `va-size-*` pairs with the more-than-4 variant as default; tiers that change no lease wording (source-of-funds exemption § 36-96.2(I), the 2027 payment plan, the 'fewer than four' records rule, the 200-unit key rule) went into education. Every VA row carries a `VA-SCOPE:` marker. The builder needs a per-state 'rental units owned' landlord attribute to pick the variant (VA log §14, Addendum M flag; Taylor noted Colorado's unit count also changes court procedure). Taylor's call (2026-09-28): two versions where wording differs, the same model as Tennessee's county pilot.
55. **Check whether the official compilation's bulk data lags the session, and overlay the update pages before any whole-code search.** Added after Virginia: the Code of Virginia Law Library title files were compiled before the 2026 session (§ 55.1-1245 history ended at 2025), so a search over them alone would have missed the 14-day pay-or-quit and 512 new sections. The official '2026 Updates' pages list every section that took effect July 1, 2026 unless noted; fetching those section-open and replacing the stale text gave a current corpus (1,464 replaced, 512 added). Record the corpus build and its control term in the log (VA log §1, §17).
56. **When a kickoff lead describes an exemption or opt-out, confirm it still exists in the current text and trace when it left.** Added after Virginia: the kickoff expected a small-landlord exemption; the two-single-family-house opt-out existed in former §§ 55-248.3:1(B) and 55-225.01(B)(1) through the 2019 enrolled acts but is absent from § 55.1-1201 as recodified and reprinted in 2022. Writing rows to an exemption that no longer exists would have left most small Virginia landlords under-covered. Where the dropping act cannot be pinned, say so (VA log §7, §12).
57. **When a statute requires a notice, consent or agreement to be SEPARATE from the lease, no lease clause can supply it; screen every shared clause that claims that right by lease text, and record the separate document as a builder gap.** Added after Alabama: entry to show the unit without consent needs a general notice 'separate from the rental agreement' signed by the tenant (Ala. Code § 35-9A-303(b)(4)); a scheduled-service notice that dispenses with entry notice must be 'separate from the lease' (§ 35-9A-303(d)); a non-single-family tenant repair agreement must be 'a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration' (§ 35-9A-204(d)(1)). The shared `landlords-access` grants a lease-based right to show the unit on 24 hours' notice, so Alabama took `landlords-access-al`. Search 'separate from the (lease|rental agreement)', 'separate writing', 'separate instrument' and 'separately signed'; record each in the state log's layout table as an Addendum M.12 separate-document gap. The reverse of instruction 48 (the lease itself as the notice). Added 2026-09-28 (AL).
58. **Where a state bans lease terms making the tenant pay the landlord's 'costs of collection', screen cost language as well as fee sentences.** Added after Alabama: Ala. Code § 35-9A-163(a)(3) bars a tenant agreement 'to pay the landlord's attorney's fees or cost of collection', with a money penalty for knowingly enforcing it (§ 35-9A-163(b)). `default-by-tenant-ks-ne` drops the prevailing-party fee sentence but keeps 'recovering ... reasonable costs and expenses', which reads as a collection-cost term, so Alabama took its own `default-by-tenant-al` with neither. Search each state's prohibited-terms section for 'collection' and read 'costs and expenses', 'collection costs' and 'at Tenant's cost' in every tagged clause. Extends instructions 32 and 49. Added 2026-09-28 (AL).
59. **When the official compilation has a structured data service, load the whole code (including pending and superseded versions) and prove the load complete against an independent section index before certifying any absence.** Added after Alabama: ALISON serves the Code of Alabama through the Legislature's GraphQL endpoint with versions keyed to effective and supersession dates, so the corpus included law effective 2026-10-01 and later; offset paging returned 49,638 records with 9 duplicated versions, and completeness was checked against the service's own title index (49,293 section ids; the 5 unmatched ids are index artifacts that the service does not return as sections). A paging API can silently skip or repeat records; count distinct ids and versions against a second source (AL log §1). Extends instructions 39 and 55. Added 2026-09-28 (AL).
60. **Screen every landlord-tenant statute for 'the lease controls' wording before writing a clause that restates it.** Added after Pennsylvania: 68 P.S. § 250.501(e) (Act § 501) lets the notice to quit 'be for a lesser time or ... be waived by the tenant if the lease so provides', and 68 P.S. § 250.505a(g) (Act § 505.1) makes a written lease control over the abandoned-property section except the protection-from-abuse hold. Each is a choice the library must make on purpose: Pennsylvania offers the waiver as an optional clause and mirrors the abandoned-property statute (PA log §6). Search 'if the lease so provides', 'unless the lease', 'except as (otherwise )?provided in the lease', 'lease shall (govern|control)' and 'otherwise agreed in writing'. Where the state has a readability or consumer-restrictions statute (instruction 61), every option taken is also a waiver to list. Added 2026-09-29 (PA).
61. **Check whether a state's plain-language or consumer-contract statute reaches residential leases, and if it requires a statement of waivers, make that statement a REQUIRED clause the builder fills from the options chosen.** Added after Pennsylvania: the Plain Language Consumer Contract Act (73 P.S. §§ 2201-2212) applies to residential leases (not contracts over $50,000, measure unstated), judges the lease as a whole on readability factors (short sentences, boldface captions, readable type), requires a statement of what the tenant could lose and of every waiver (73 P.S. § 2205(d)), and gives actual loss plus $100 and fees (73 P.S. § 2207(a)) with a good-faith defense (73 P.S. § 2208(a)(3)). `consumer-restrictions-statement-pa` carries a bracketed waiver list; shared clauses that disclaim landlord liability (`tenants-property-insurance`) were swapped for variants that do not. Record the builder need (Addendum M: the waiver list fills from the chosen options) and the readability check as a product flag. Added 2026-09-29 (PA).
62. **Where the official site does not print the compiler's section numbers, confirm each number against an official mapping before using it, and cite by the act's own section where you cannot.** Added after Pennsylvania: palegis.us prints unconsolidated acts by their own section numbers only; Purdon's (P.S.) numbers are a private compilation. The 1951 Act's 68 P.S. § 250.NNN numbering follows the Act's section numbers, with letter suffixes for the decimal sections (Act § 505.1 is 68 P.S. § 250.505a; Act § 511.1 is § 250.511a), and is always given with the Act section in parentheses (kickoff rule); the CO alarm act, the service-animal act, the ETA, the Expedited Eviction Act and the Housing Authorities Law are cited as 'section N' because no official source tied them to Purdon's numbers. A kickoff lead's P.S. number that cannot be tied to an official act ('68 P.S. § 399.1') is a text question for Taylor, not a citation (PA log §6, question A). Added 2026-09-29 (PA).
63. **Read the court rules for eviction procedure whole, including their 'Acts of Assembly suspended' rule and pending amendments in the official Bulletin, before stating any eviction timing from the statute.** Added after Pennsylvania: Pa.R.Civ.P.M.D.J. 581 suspends Acts of Assembly inconsistent with the Chapter 500 rules and Rule 582 keeps the Rent Withholding Act in force; the hearing window (Rule 504), order-for-possession timing (Rules 515, 517, 519), local mediation (Rule 504.1, from 2025-10-01), the domestic-violence stay (Rule 514.1, amended 2026-04-01) and supersedeas (Rule 1008) all come from the rules, and the order at 56 Pa.B. 2569 (effective 2026-11-01) changes only commentary within Chapter 500, plus fee-waiver and other wording in Rules 206.1, 1002, 1008 and 1016. Confessed ejectment on residential leases is abolished by a note to Pa.R.C.P. 2970, not by statute. Flag every rule-based statement as non-statute (instruction 16). Added 2026-09-29 (PA).
64. **Save every primary text to disk as it is read, and treat a draft whose sources were not saved as recall.** Added after Pennsylvania: a same-day draft of this pass existed with row text but no log and no saved sources; re-checked against primary text reopened and saved, it needed 23 corrections (PA log §13), including wrong section numbers, a Fiscal Code cite and unsourced Fire and Panic Act claims. The whole-code search battery was re-run and its output saved as JSON before the log was written, which also turned up a new finding (53 Pa.C.S. § 6113). Keep one file per section or act under the state's source folder, and copy every count in the log from saved output, never from memory. Added 2026-09-29 (PA).
65. **A statutory limit on the landlord's conduct is an education row, not a lease clause, unless a statute requires the lease to contain the text (or to be given in writing, with the lease as the vehicle), or the lease must make a choice the statute leaves open.** Set by Taylor on 2026-09-29, in the Pennsylvania pass. The limit applies whether or not the lease mentions it, and restating it in the lease invites promises the statute does not make: Pennsylvania's draft cap clause promised a year-two refund that 68 P.S. § 250.511a (Act § 511.1) does not require. Where the landlord enters a figure the limit governs (a deposit amount, a fee), the builder enforces it (Addendum M). PA follows CO, KS, NE, ND and SD (`edu-security-deposit-cap-*`). CA, NV, AZ, NC, GA and AL still carry cap lease clauses, and their cleanup is with Claude Code, with a per-row checklist in PA log §9.2. The same rule reaches other restating clauses (deposit return and holding, CO alarm allocation); how far to apply it is a library-architecture decision pending with Taylor and Claude Code. Screen each new state's rows against this rule, and record which statutes do require lease text. Added 2026-09-29 (PA).
66. **Run the three-bucket test on every row before giving it a `rule_type`, and record why each lease clause belongs in the lease.** Added 2026-09-29 by Taylor, after the Pennsylvania pass showed the test had never reached this checklist: it lived only in the CO log (§7), so every state from Ohio on classified rows without it, and six states shipped deposit caps as lease clauses. The test, in full:
    - **A row is a lease clause only if it passes at least one of:** (1) **REQUIRED_DISCLOSURE**: a statute requires the lease to contain the text, or requires it in writing where the lease is the practical vehicle; (2) **CONSTRAINED_TERM**: a term the landlord must state (rent, late fee, entry notice) where law limits what it can be; the clause states the landlord's own choice, normally a placeholder the landlord fills, never the statute's limit; (3) **SERVES_LANDLORD**: a term the landlord benefits from the tenant agreeing to in writing (a tenant duty, an opt-in right, a choice the statute leaves to the lease).
    - **Otherwise it is a `LANDLORD_EDUCATION` row:** real law the landlord should know that applies whether or not the lease says it (caps, penalties, deadlines, landlord duties). Instruction 65 is the cap case of this rule.
    - **Quick screen first (Taylor, 2026-09-29): is this clause a maximum, minimum, limit, ceiling or floor, and who sets it?** If a statute sets it, the row is probably education (a strong default, not a guarantee). If the landlord or lease sets it, it is a clause. The two exceptions: a statute that lets the lease choose within its limit (Colorado's bed-bug entry notice, a return period of "30 days or up to 60 if the lease says") makes the landlord's chosen figure a clause; a statute that requires the limit itself to be disclosed in the lease makes it a required disclosure.
    - **Restatement check, asked of every row:** is this clause just restating the statute? If so, what does it add? If it adds nothing, it is education. If it adds something, only the addition stays in the lease, and it must be one of the three criteria above; the restated part moves to education (split the row). If the restatement is wrong or promises more than the statute (Pennsylvania's draft cap clause promised a year-two refund the statute does not require), flag it wherever it lands.
    - **Record the answer in `lease_clause_basis`** (a column of `lease-clauses.csv`): one or more of `REQUIRED_DISCLOSURE: <statute>`, `CONSTRAINED_TERM`, `SERVES_LANDLORD`, separated by ` | `. Required for every active `LEASE_CLAUSE` row; blank for every other row. A real lease's wording is evidence for how to word a term, not a basis on its own.
    - **Surface borderline calls to Taylor** with the proposed bucket and a one-line reason (CO log §7: over-include with stated reasoning, never silently omit).
    - **Claude Code runs `python3 scripts/clause-library/check-clause-basis.py lease-clauses.csv` at every sync**; it fails on a missing or invalid basis, so a state can't be synced without the test having been applied. Instruction 24's deposit-return family check now means the state's deposit rules are covered as a clause or as education, not that a lease clause must exist.

## KS RE-AUDIT RESULTS — 2026-08-29/30 (v57 → v62)

**Kansas is closed.** 113 KS-tagged rows, 112 VERIFIED, 1 NEEDS_REVIEW (`assistance-animal-accommodation`, blocked on Nebraska).

### ⚠️ INSTRUCTION — never carry a denominator forward; derive it and state the extraction rule

**Origin.** Pass 1 of the KS canvass worked from the CO re-audit, WY re-audit, and ND/NE new-topic sections — the sections a re-audit naturally reaches for — canvassed **31** rows, and reported "31 of 31 resolved," when the file held far more. Pass 2 caught it. The substantive exposure was small (the others were largely resolved in Kansas's original pass) but the completeness claim was measured against a subset the session selected itself.

**Amended 2026-08-31 (NE re-audit), after the rule's first inheritance nearly reproduced the failure it was written to prevent.** The KS re-audit recorded "**73** distinct topic rows" as a bare figure. The NE re-audit session was handed 73 in its prompt and, had it accepted the number, would have under-counted by eight. 73 was wrong two separate ways:

1. **Stale.** It was counted *during* the KS pass, before that same pass appended its own nine new canvass rows. Any figure written into this file is obsolete the moment the session writing it adds a row.
2. **Measured differently.** It counted deduplicated distinct topic labels; a row-based extraction counts rows. Neither is wrong — they answer different questions.

Two careful independent extractions during the NE session produced **81** and **82**, differing on header-detection rules. That disagreement is itself the finding: **a bare number cannot be authoritative, because the count depends on a rule that the number alone does not carry.** Do not chase the residual ±1; record it.

**The rule.**

1. **Never carry a denominator forward** from a prior session's prompt, a prior log, or an earlier line in this file. Every figure in this file is a historical record of what one session counted under one rule on one date — not a current fact.
2. **Derive it fresh from this file, programmatically, at every pass** — including pass 2 of the same session, independently of pass 1.
3. **State the extraction rule alongside the number.** At minimum: what counts as a topic row, which tables are included or excluded and why, and how header rows are detected. A denominator without its rule is not reproducible and is not a claim.
4. **Record disagreement rather than reconciling it.** If a second extraction differs, report both figures and the rule difference that produced them. Do not silently adopt one, and do not reconcile to a number supplied in a prompt.

**Extraction rule used by the NE re-audit (2026-08-31), for reference — reproduce or supersede, don't inherit:** every markdown table row in this file, excluding separator rows and excluding header rows detected by a first cell matching `topic|layer|row|new topic`; further excluding the 12-row "Status corrections — these rows were stale for Kansas" table, whose entries restate topics already present elsewhere in the file rather than introducing distinct ones. **Result: 81 topic rows** (72 pre-dating the KS re-audit, plus that pass's 9 additions). A parallel extraction under a slightly different header rule returned 82.

Fourth instance in this project of a completeness claim failing on scope rather than on research.

### Methodology lessons added

1. **Read section titles for provisions the retrieved body text may have truncated.** 31-162's (g)/(h) shields were recovered only by chasing the title's reference to "certain evidence inadmissible; insurance payments not affected."
2. **Resolving one flag requires reading the whole section.** 58-2570(a)'s 7-day week-to-week notice was found only while resolving the 15-day military figure.
3. **A bill that becomes a Substitute must be re-read in enacted form.** The KS eviction row was built from a summary blending the introduced bill with the enacted one — same failure as CO's carpet-lookback (superseded draft read as enacted text), one level up.
4. **A citation-existence screen cannot catch a valid citation described wrongly.** The material KS error this re-audit found (39-1112) was not a citation error.
5. **Don't cite statute sections for a brand-new law until the Revisor publishes the amendments.** K.S.A. 61-3804/61-3806/61-3807 show no 2026 amendment; cite Sub. HB 2357 directly.

Pass-2 rule, deliberately different implementation: segment into contiguous table blocks, drop separators, treat each block's **first row** as its header structurally rather than by keyword. Both returned 81. Taylor's independent extraction returned **82**; recorded, not reconciled, per the amended instruction above.

LB150 predates the original pass — research miss, not a currency lapse. |
