### Methodology lessons added

1. **Read every section of a multi-section act, especially the one addressed to your own audience.** The CO-alarm error came from reading §§76-603/604/605 (construction and sellers) and stopping before §76-606 (landlords). Four of this session's findings share this single root — smoke detector, §81-5,142, holdover/possession, CO alarms.
2. **A partial quotation from a secondary compilation is not the section.** An NCSL summary quoting only §81-5,142(1) led *this re-audit* to invent a coverage gap that subsections (2) and (3) closed. Caught only because the row was parked at `NEEDS_REVIEW` rather than shipped — over-include-and-flag caught the auditor's own error.
3. **Time-based measures and multipliers are not interchangeable.** "Three months' periodic rent" ≠ "3× periodic rent" outside a monthly tenancy. Paraphrasing a damages formula loses the distinction; quote the statute's construction.
4. **A prohibited-provisions section may not be the complete list.** See §76-1413(9).
5. **When the same error shape appears twice in one session, stop and get primary text.** The CO-alarm suspicion was flagged rather than acted on precisely because §81-5,142 had just gone wrong the same way; §5a.2 was invoked instead of a third search, and the primary text showed the problem was worse than suspected.
6. **A logged-only absence is invisible to future canvasses.** The all-in-pricing row was resolved in this checklist and never entered the library. Confirmed absences need CSV rows, not prose.
7. **The checklist's own main tables can go stale while the CSV is corrected.** The 49-row re-verification found four NE column entries still carrying errors this session had already fixed in the library — the holdover and possession-delay `3×` figures, the 'tracks federal only' protected-class entry, and the carbon-monoxide 'only new construction' scope. Because the checklist *is* the canvass instrument, a future state would have inherited wrong Nebraska benchmarks from it while the CSV said otherwise. Fixing a CSV row is not finishing the job; the checklist entry that sourced it has to move too.
8. **The denominator contains a genuine duplicate topic**, which explains why row-counting and distinct-label-counting diverge rather than merely differing by an off-by-one. 'Returned/dishonored check fee cap' and 'Genuinely new: returned-check-fee cap (candidate, investigated)' are the same subject occupying two counted rows in two sections. A deduplicated count legitimately returns a smaller number than a row count. Neither is wrong; this is concrete evidence for why a bare denominator cannot be authoritative without its extraction rule. Left in place deliberately — merging them would silently change the denominator again.

### Method findings from the MN re-audit

- **ARCHIVED-VERSION TRAP — recommend a standing screen.** Three instances this session: my own §504B.206 "fax" delivery method (pre-2014 text), MN's earlier log citing §504B.135(b) (removed by 2023 c 52 art 19 s 97), and §484.014's repealed "sufficiently without basis" expungement test. **Neither the citation-existence screen nor the notes-field screen catches this** — the section exists, the text is genuine, it simply is not the law anymore. Rule: treat any revisor URL containing a year path or version timestamp as historical until confirmed against the current-cite URL. Apply **extra** scrutiny where the stale text is landlord-favorable, since that is the direction least likely to be questioned in a landlord-facing library.
- **SECTION-TITLE TRAP.** §504B.120 is titled "Prohibited Fees" and prohibits nothing. Resolving a topic from a section title is unsafe.
- **ROW-PRESENCE ASYMMETRY CHECK — recommend adding to the canvass method.** "Does another state have a row on this topic that this state lacks?" would have caught the §504B.181 and §504B.182 gaps for free, and it runs in both directions: MN now has findings (the disclosure maintenance bar) that KS and NE may be missing.
- **PROOF-OF-ABSENCE IS SYSTEMIC, NOT INCIDENTAL.** Pass 1 found a large group of topics adjudicated in MN's log and never given a CSV row, plus three cases where the log asserted coverage that did not exist — fair housing, retaliation, and domestic violence, the last of which recorded "already covered" and was self-sealing against future canvasses.
- **KEYWORD PROBES DO NOT SUBSTITUTE FOR ADJUDICATION.** A programmatic keyword-overlap probe of topic labels against MN rows returned near-total apparent coverage. It was discarded; the real pass required listing every MN row and matching by hand.

### Open for MN

- ~~§504B.111 / 2025 HF 1648~~ **RESOLVED 2026-09-03 on primary text: HF 1648 was NOT enacted.** History line ends at 1Sp2019 c 1 art 6 s 56. No no-unilateral-amendment rule and no treble-damages remedy exist in current law. **Method note:** the bill's 'identify the specific unit' sentence appears in current text because it came from the 2019 amendment, not from HF 1648 — bills reproduce existing language alongside proposed additions, and in plain text the two are indistinguishable. **Add to the archived-version screen: a pending bill is not evidence of enactment, and overlap between bill text and current text is not partial enactment. Check the history line.**
- §325G.35 (AG review), §325G.16 full text, §504B.151 subd. 2 (holder-agreement exception), §484.014 subd. 3(a) clause (5).
- **SD is also not a column in this file.** MN and SD were both missing; MN is now added. SD remains absent and should be added when SD is re-audited.

## ND RE-AUDIT RESULTS — 2026-09-06 (v100 → v112)

Sixth state re-audited at higher settings. **Six for six: every re-audited state has surfaced errors that shipped as `VERIFIED`.** ND produced ten, two of them the worst shapes yet seen (a fabricated statutory grounds list, and a `REQUIRED` lease clause that was asserted "Present — full mechanics confirmed" in this checklist while no CSV row existed at all).

Plus the known semantic duplicate. Disagreement recorded, not reconciled.

**ND's column status, correcting the session premise:** ND *was* already a column in the eight original tables and the ND new-topics table. It was absent from the six sections added since — **56 of 110 rows**. Those are answered below.

| `edu-holdover-damages-nd` (new) | Checklist asserted ND had **"no multiplier at all."** Wrong. §§ 32-03-27 (double the rent) and 32-03-28 (**double the yearly value for the time of withholding**) — in Title 32, not Title 47. |

### Method findings from the ND re-audit

1. **A scope boundary can produce an OMISSION rather than a misstatement.** The K.2 boundary re-examined was **tenancy type** — verdict **wrong**. ND distinguishes tenancy type in six places (§§ 47-16-05, -15(1) vs -15(2), -19, -20, -06.1, -07). The consequence was not a bad row but **no row at all**: ND had no termination-notice clause whatsoever. The four prior re-audits all found errors *inside* scope; this is a distinct failure mode.
2. **The canvass can only find what the checklist lists.** ND's missing termination-notice clause survived an original pass and a first canvass because **this file has no generic "termination notice period" topic row**. That is a defect in the checklist, not in ND's execution.
3. **Naming a trap does not confer immunity to it.** This session warned against confusing § 47-16-19 "lodgings" with ch. 23-09 "lodging establishment" — and the *next flag written in the same row* misattributed a lodging-establishment rule (ch. 33-33-05, "Law Implemented: NDCC 23-09-02.1") to the general residential statute.
4. **Read the sections your section points to.** `dv-lease-release-nd` (moved to `edu-dv-lease-release-nd` by the 2026-09-29 scrub) was written this session from correct § 47-16-17.1 text and was still materially over-broad, because § 14-07.1-01 — the definition that section incorporates — went unread. Same shape as reading only the subsection carrying a figure.
5. **A checklist entry asserting "Present — full mechanics confirmed" is not evidence a row exists.** ND's DV termination clause was recorded as present here and existed nowhere in the CSV. Recommend a standing **checklist-to-CSV reconciliation screen**: for every row marked Present, assert a matching CSV row exists.
6. **Repealed-out-from-under is a distinct citation failure.** § 14-02.4-18 is live, correctly quoted, and no longer reaches housing. A citation-existence screen passes it; only reading the chapter's repeal history catches it.
7. **Post-write assertions catch what review does not.** The first v101 write left `states` blank on five new rows — they would have displayed nowhere. Caught by the tag-count assertion, not by reading the diff.

Code art. 45-18~~ — **art. 45-18 RESOLVED 2026-09-06.** § 23-13-15's "fire marshal standards" resolve to the State Building Code fire provisions plus the **International Fire Code 2021** as modified (N.D. Admin. Code § 45-18-01-04) — **privately published model codes, not freely readable** (`edu-fire-code-standard-nd`). Electronic notice regime: **absent**, and § 47-16-17.1(3) enumerates mail, facsimile or in person for a DV notice **without listing email** while § 47-16-07 uses a permissive functional standard — an asymmetry worth knowing (`edu-no-electronic-notice-regime-nd`). Freeze-date incorporation: **present, but not in the animal provisions** — § 14-02.5-06(3)(c) freezes to ANSI A117.1 (1986) and the fire code to IFC 2021 (`edu-frozen-standard-incorporation-nd`). Protected-class inquiry and record ban: **absent**; nearest provision is § 14-02.5-03 (Publication), which reaches notices and advertisements, not inquiries (`edu-no-protected-class-inquiry-ban-nd`).
- Animal carve-out vs fair-housing carve-out **misalignment candidate** (§ 14-02.5-09(2) vs §§ 47-16-07.5/-07.6).
- ~~Cross-state tenancy-type sensitivity~~ — **SCREEN RUN 2026-09-06**, results in the dedicated section above. Assumption wrong in six of seven states.
- ~~Fee-shifting mutuality consolidation across CO/WY/KS/NE/MN/ND~~ — **RESOLVED 2026-09-06.** Five distinct architectures, not one question: CO requires mutual drafting (one-way clause void); MN imposes mutuality by operation of law regardless of text; **KS and NE ban fee clauses outright in either direction** (`default-by-tenant` correctly untagged for both, and a library-wide check confirms zero LEASE_CLAUSE rows tagged KS or NE carry attorney-fee language); ND awards to "the prevailing party" by statute (§ 47-16-13.6); WY follows the American Rule. **One open flag: Wyoming.** Its Supreme Court requires a contract to "unequivocally provide" for fee recovery, and `default-by-tenant` hedges twice — *"to the extent permitted under applicable law"* and *"may recover"*. That phrasing may not suffice, leaving a WY landlord with no fee recovery at all. The hedge is what makes the clause safe to share with CO and MN, so **any fix must be a WY-specific override, not an edit to the shared text.**

## CROSS-STATE TENANCY-TYPE SENSITIVITY SCREEN — 2026-09-06

**Origin.** The ND re-audit's Addendum K.2 boundary re-examination found the library had silently assumed every tenancy is a whole-dwelling monthly or fixed-term lease. ND punished that assumption. Taylor directed this screen be run across the other six states rather than folded into their future re-audits.

**Question, per state:** does the state distinguish tenancy type in notice periods, rent-payment defaults, or scope thresholds — and do our rows reflect it?

### Library side — do our rows carry a termination-notice provision, and is it tenancy-type aware?

| State | Termination-notice row? | Sub-monthly aware? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CO** | `month-to-month-notice-co-exempt`, `month-to-month-notice-co-covered` | ~~No — flat **21 days**~~ → **corrected to the five-tier scheme (v117)** | **ERROR CONFIRMED AND FIXED — see below** |
| **WY** | ~~None at all~~ → `edu-no-statutory-termination-notice-wy` (v118) | Yes — common-law scaling stated | **GAP FILLED** |
| **KS** | `edu-military-termination-notice-ks` | **Yes** — 7-day week-to-week | Clean (caught by KS re-audit) |
| **NE** | `edu-periodic-termination-notice-ne` | **Yes** — 7-day week-to-week, 30-day month-to-month | Clean (caught by NE re-audit) |
| **MN** | ~~None at all~~ → `edu-tenancy-at-will-termination-notice-mn` (v118) | Yes — statutory formula, not a figure | **GAP FILLED** |
| **SD** | `edu-tenancy-at-will-termination-sd` | No — 15-day tenancy-at-will only | **ANSWER FOUND, routed to the SD session — see below** |
| **ND** | `termination-notice-nd` + `edu-tenancy-type-notice-nd` | Yes, in the companion education row | Clean (this session) |

### CO — HIGH PRIORITY FLAG, not yet a confirmed error

**C.R.S. § 13-40-107(1) sets a five-tier notice scheme**, not a single figure:

| Tenancy | Notice |
|---|---|
| One year or longer | **91 days** |
| Six months or longer but less than a year | **28 days** |
| One month or longer but less than six months | **21 days** |
| One week or longer but less than one month, or tenancy at will | **3 days** |
| Less than one week | **1 day** |

Both shipped CO clauses state **21 days flat** — the third tier only. If "tenancy" is measured by **duration of occupancy** (which is how CO practitioner material reads it: *"Determine the tenancy length to identify the correct notice period: 21 days (1–6 months), 28 days (6–12 months), 91 days (1+ year)"*), then a Colorado month-to-month tenant of two years is owed **91 days**, and our clause understates it by seventy days.

**Why this is flagged rather than corrected here.** Three reasons, all deliberate:
1. The **duration-of-occupancy vs rental-interval** reading of "a tenancy of…" needs confirmation against primary text and CO case law. The statute is old (L. 1885) with a long amendment history — the 1–6 month tier read *seven days* until 2017.
2. CO carries an **HB24-1098 just-cause overlay** for 12+ month tenancies that interacts with any no-cause non-renewal notice, and both shipped rows are already split into `-exempt` / `-covered` variants because of it.
3. **Editing CO rows from an ND session would violate Addendum E discipline** — a cosmetic repair is one thing, a substantive notice-period rewrite is CO re-verification and belongs in a CO session.

**RESOLVED AND CORRECTED 2026-09-06 (v117), at Taylor's direction** — there being no planned future CO session. Current § 13-40-107 read from primary text as amended by **HB24-1098 (ch. 113, § 5, effective 2024-04-19)**.

**The duration reading is settled by the statute's own words:** § 13-40-107(1) requires notice *"based on the length of the applicable tenancy described in subsection (2)."* HB24-1098 also inserted **"at least"** before each figure — the tiers are floors, not fixed periods.

Both CO clauses corrected. **Three distinct defects, not one:**

1. **Flat 21 days.** Corrected to the full five-tier scheme in both rows. A month-to-month tenant of two years was owed 91 days; the clause understated by seventy.
2. **`-covered` was doubly wrong on its own terms** — even inside its stated "first 12 months" window, months six through twelve require at least 28 days, not 21.
3. **`-covered` had the wrong party.** As amended, § 13-40-107(1) grants the right to *"A landlord of nonresidential real property or a residential premises described in section 38-12-1302(1)(a), (1)(b), (1)(d), (1)(e), or (1)(f) **or a tenant of any property or premises**."* A **covered residential landlord is not in that list**; a tenant of any property is. The section supplies a tenant-side route on a covered property and no landlord-side one. Clause rewritten accordingly.

**Also caught, and separately rowed as `edu-fixed-term-nonrenewal-notice-co`:** the pre-2024 text excused notice *"from or to"* a tenant whose term ended at a time certain. Current § 13-40-107(4) excuses it **only "from a tenant."** The words *"or to"* are gone. **The common landlord assumption that a fixed-term lease simply expires with no notice required is no longer correct in Colorado** — § 13-40-107(1) expressly covers electing "to not renew a fixed term tenancy," and the tiers apply, so declining renewal on a year-plus tenancy takes at least 91 days' notice.

**Left open and deliberately not asserted:** by what route, if any, a covered residential landlord may terminate without cause during months 0–12. § 38-12-1303's just-cause requirement attaches at 12 months, but § 13-40-107(1) does not name covered residential landlords at all. § 38-12-1301 et seq. and § 38-12-1302 were **not read** this session. The clause no longer asserts a landlord no-cause right in that window — the safe direction — but the question is open.

**Scope discipline:** edited from the ND re-audit session at Taylor's express direction. Per Addendum E this is a targeted correction of the notice-period holdings only. **It is not a CO re-audit**, and no other CO holding was reviewed.

### WY and MN — no termination-notice row exists at all

Neither state has any row stating how a periodic tenancy is terminated. This is the **same omission shape** ND exhibited: not a wrong row, an absent one, invisible because this checklist has no generic *"termination notice period"* topic row for a canvass to hit.

MN is the more likely to bite: § 504B.135 scales the notice to *"the interval between the time rent is due or three months, whichever is shorter"* — a rule that is **inherently tenancy-type-scaled**, so a single stated figure could not capture it even if one existed.

### WY and MN — gaps filled (v118)

**WY: confirmed absent, and the absence is the finding.** Wyoming sets **no statutory notice period** for ending a periodic tenancy — not month-to-month, not week-to-week, not a periodic tenancy of a year or more. Evidence is affirmative rather than absence-of-mention: a structured state chart returns "No statute" across all four categories, and Nolo states outright that neither party is required by statute to give notice. The ubiquitous "30 days" is **common-law practice, not statute** — and the common-law rule is itself tenancy-type scaled (one full rental period, terminating at the start of a new period), so a landlord applying "30 days" to a weekly tenancy is wrong by a factor of four. The row says the 30-day figure is non-statutory expressly, and states the rule at practice-level confidence since no WY case fixing it was located.

**MN: the purest example the screen found of why a flat figure cannot work.** § 504B.135 states **no number at all** — notice must be *"at least as long as the interval between the time rent is due or three months, whichever is less."* That is a **formula**. Any row saying "MN requires X days" is wrong for every tenancy whose rent interval isn't X. Note *"whichever is less"* makes three months a **ceiling**, not a floor.

**A repeal caught in the same read:** the section formerly carried a second paragraph giving a **14-day notice to quit** for unpaid rent on a tenancy at will. Struck by 2023 Minn. Laws ch. 52, art. 19, § 97, effective 2024-01-01, applying to leases entered into or renewed on or after that date. The current official text carries no subdivision designations at all, confirming the deletion. **Justia's 2013 and 2016 versions still show the "(a)" designation** — a live K.4 archived-version trap for anyone reading a mirror.

**Open on the MN row, flagged not asserted:** MN case law reportedly fixes a **counting rule** for when the notice takes effect, traced by a secondary source to 1891 authority. Not located in primary form, deliberately omitted from the row body. A landlord could satisfy the length requirement and still serve ineffective notice on timing.

### SD — answer found, routed to the SD session rather than fixed here

**§ 43-32-15** supplies what `edu-tenancy-at-will-termination-sd` does not: a hiring for a term not specified by the parties is deemed renewed unless a party gives notice of intention to terminate *"at least as long before the expiration thereof as the term of the hiring itself, not exceeding one month."* **Scaled to the term, capped at one month** — so a week-to-week SD tenancy takes about a week's notice.

**That is structurally identical to ND's § 47-16-15(1)**, and the reason is visible in the source lines: SD's chapter traces to *CivC 1877* — the Dakota Territory Civil Code, which both Dakotas inherited. **SD and ND leasing chapters are near-parallel by descent.** § 43-32-12 (rent timing: agricultural / lodging / other) mirrors ND § 47-16-20; § 43-32-13 (30-day modification notice, tenant's 15-day response) mirrors ND § 47-16-07 and § 47-16-15(3).

**Directed input to the SD session, which is next:** ND findings are *candidates* for SD and vice versa, but must be verified rather than inherited — the shared ancestry makes assumed transfer especially tempting and especially dangerous. Note one confirmed divergence already: SD gives tenants at will who are active servicemembers **two months' written notice** (§ 43-8-8), where ND has **no state military provision at all**.

SD is also still not a column in this file.

### Screen conclusions

1. **The assumption was wrong in every state that had not already caught it.** CO carried a confirmed error across two shipped lease clauses; WY and MN had outright omissions, now filled; SD's answer is found and routed to its own session. Only KS and NE were clean, and both only because their own re-audits happened to catch it. **Six of seven states were affected.**
2. **Add a generic "Termination notice period — and does it scale with tenancy type?" row to this checklist's main tables.** Its absence is why three states shipped without the clause and no canvass noticed. This is the second checklist-structure defect this session (the first being that a checklist entry can assert coverage the CSV lacks).
3. **A flat notice figure in a clause is a tenancy-type assumption in disguise.** Any row stating "X days' notice" without stating what tenancy it applies to should be treated as suspect until checked.

Running the item-6a reconciliation in reverse (every SD-tagged CSV row must map to a topic here) surfaced a defect in **this file**, not in any state's research. **53 of 88 SD rows are referenced nowhere in this checklist.** Most are Tier A boilerplate and correctly absent — `keys`, `severability`, `notices` are clauses, not named topics. But the reverse check also shows that **several universal, core subjects have no topic row at all, for any state:**

| Missing topic | Evidence |
|---|---|

The file has *Deposit amount cap*, *Deposit installment-payment right*, *Last-month's-rent restriction*, and *Successor-owner bound* — but nothing for the return deadline itself. |
| **Landlord habitability / repair duty** | Zero labels match "repair duty". Only *Alternate housing during habitability failure* and a MN-specific non-waivability row exist — both downstream of the duty, neither the duty. |

| **Meth/contamination disclosure** | No topic row; the only "meth" substring match is *Payment-method fee ban*. NE (backfill 2026-09-27): **PRESENT — and far more than disclosure. Whole scheme was absent from the library until 2026-09-27.** §§71-2432 to 71-2435 (Chapter 71). There is **no disclosure duty as such**, but there are three others and a landlord right: **owner must REPORT** a known clandestine drug lab to local law enforcement or the State Patrol as soon as practicable (§71-2433); **owner must not permit human habitation or use** until rehabilitation is complete and the local public health department releases the property, knowing violation = **civil penalty up to $1,000** enforced by DHHS (§71-2434(3)); the health department **may charge the owner** for monitoring costs (§71-2434(2)); and the owner **may terminate the lease on THREE DAYS' written notice, "notwithstanding any other provision of law,"** to rehabilitate (§71-2435). **Search-method warning for every other state: `methamphetamine laboratory` returned 0 hits; `clandestine` returned all four sections.** `edu-clandestine-drug-lab-ne`. MN (backfill 2026-09-27): No landlord disclosure duty. §152.0275 subd. 2 instead: a health department or sheriff SHALL prohibit occupancy or use until assessed and remediated to MDH guidelines; contractor verifies within five days and is liable to the owner for a bad certification (six-year limit); and the AUTHORITY records an affidavit that "discloses to any potential transferee" the lab history, which the recorder must record so it appears in an ordinary title search. TERM TRAP: "clandestine drug lab" and "drug laboratory" both return 0 — the statute says "clandestine lab site" and only "methamphetamine" finds it (`edu-meth-lab-property-orders-mn`). |
| **Month-to-month modification notice** | Only a narrow MN-specific *rent-increase notice gap on a written month-to-month lease*. |

**Why this matters, and it is not academic.** The SD re-audit's headline finding was that `security-deposit-return-sd` (moved to `edu-security-deposit-itemized-accounting-sd` by the 2026-09-29 scrub) shipped a superseded **two-week** deadline after SL 2026, ch 179 changed it to twenty-one days. **A two-pass named-topic canvass executed perfectly would never have caught it, because this checklist has no row for the deposit-return deadline to check.**

**Root cause — accretion bias.** This file grew by adding a topic whenever some state's law *surprised* the researcher. Exotic and edge provisions therefore have rich coverage: double-letting, EV charging, eviction-record sealing, immigrant tenant protection. **Universal obligations never surprised anyone, so they never earned a row** — and they are exactly the provisions every state has, that get amended, and that ship into every lease. The checklist is densest where risk is lowest.

**Section now created** — see *CORE OBLIGATIONS* below. SD is filled from primary text read during the SD re-audit. **The other six states are deliberately left as `NOT CANVASSED`**: their statuses cannot be inherited from their decision logs, because under this project's own re-audit standard a log's assertions are claims to verify rather than facts, and because the whole point of this finding is that these topics were never canvassed for any state. Filling them from memory or from prior logs would reproduce the defect in a new location. Each state needs a real pass.

- `security-deposit-interest-oh` (moved to `edu-security-deposit-interest-oh` by the 2026-09-29 scrub) is a **rewrite**, not a repair.

| **Landlord habitability / repair duty** | **Implied in every rental agreement, with the tightest response clock of the five states** — §38-12-503(1): the landlord is deemed to warrant the premises **fit for human habitation**. Breach where the premises is uninhabitable under §38-12-505 or otherwise unfit, **or** in a condition **materially interfering with the tenant's life, health, or safety**, the landlord has notice, and then **fails to COMMENCE remedial action within 24 HOURS** (life/health/safety) or **72 HOURS** (uninhabitable) — §38-12-503(2)(b)(I). Also breached by commencing and then failing to continue, or failing to completely remedy within a reasonable time. §38-12-505(4) supplies a **rebuttable presumption** that listed conditions materially interfere — lack of waterproofing/weather protection, hazardous gas piping or appliances, inadequate running or hot water, lack of functioning heating, and others; the landlord may rebut by showing no material interference (§38-12-505(5)). **§38-12-505(2)(a): the premises must be fit BEFORE leasing**, and leasing a non-compliant unit is itself a breach. Tenant-misconduct carve-out applies. **§38-12-503(4) adds displacement obligations no other canvassed state has** — comparable alternative dwelling within stated distance limits, hotel, **per diems for meals where no full kitchen is provided after 48 hours**, and reimbursement of storage and travel; the hotel obligation ends after 60 days. Environmental-public-health-event remediation standards and documentation duties at §38-12-505(1)(b)(XIII) | **A short standard, twice narrowed.** §1-21-1202(a): the unit must be maintained **safe and sanitary and fit for human habitation**, with **operational electrical, heating and plumbing and hot and cold running water unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties** — seasonal units such as summer cabins not intended to have such amenities are exempt. §1-21-1203(a) adds four duties: do not rent unless reasonably safe, sanitary and fit; maintain common areas; maintain electrical, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water; and maintain other appliances **only as specifically contracted**. **Narrowed twice over**: §1-21-1202(c) — the article **does not apply to breakage, malfunctions or other conditions which do not materially affect the physical health or safety of the ordinary renter**; and §1-21-1203(c) — the owner need not remedy any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees **by inappropriate use or misuse**. | **Tenant remedy for failure to repair** | **The widest remedy set of the five states, and the only one with punitive damages.** §38-12-507(1): the tenant may **terminate without any liability or financial penalty** on **10 to 60 days' written notice** stating the unremedied conditions, the intent to terminate, and a termination date at least ten days out. Or assert **claim or counterclaim** for actual damages **including any reduction in the fair rental value** during the period of uninhabitability, **plus court costs, reasonable attorney fees, PUNITIVE damages, and any other damages ordered**. Or obtain **preliminary or permanent injunctive relief including specific performance**, with the court retaining **continuing jurisdiction** to ensure compliance. Beyond the tenant's own remedies: **§38-12-512 enforcement by the ATTORNEY GENERAL** with penalties, and **§38-12-513 receivership of residential housing**. *Contrast: ND repair-and-deduct; SD repair-and-deduct/vacate/escrow; MN court-administered escrow; KS terminate-or-sue* | **A two-notice ladder ending in circuit court — richer than the earlier entry recorded.** Available only to a renter in compliance with §§1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205 (§1-21-1206(a)). Step 1, §1-21-1203(b): renter must be **current on all payments** and have **reasonable cause supported by evidence**, then advise the owner in writing of the condition and the remedial action requested, **served by certified mail** or per §1-21-1003; the owner must within a reasonable time either commence correction **or notify the renter in writing that the claim is disputed**. Step 2, §1-21-1206(b): a **"notice to repair or correct condition"** reciting the first notice, stating the elapsed time, demanding correction, and warning that **court action follows in 3 days**. Step 3, §1-21-1206(c): **civil action in circuit court**; on a showing of unreasonable refusal or failure to use due diligence the court may award **costs, damages and affirmative relief**, with damages expressly including **rent improperly retained or collected**, and relief including **termination or an order directing repairs**. On judicial termination the renter gets the rent balance and deposit **within 30 days** and must vacate between 10 and 20 days (§1-21-1206(d)). **No repair-and-deduct, no escrow, no self-help.** Counterweight: **§1-21-1203(d) lets the OWNER refuse repair and terminate** where cost is unreasonable in light of the rent, on 10–20 days' notice for the renter to find substitute housing *Verified from **wyoleg.gov**, 2024 Wyoming Statutes, Title 1 ch. 21 art. 12 — full article read* | **Neither self-help nor escrow — a fourth architecture.** §58-2559(a): on material noncompliance with the lease, or noncompliance with §58-2553 **materially affecting health and safety**, the tenant serves written notice specifying the acts and omissions and stating the lease terminates on a rent-paying date **not less than 30 days** after receipt. **But (a)(1): if the breach is remediable and the landlord adequately initiates a good-faith effort to remedy within 14 days, the lease does NOT terminate** — and on a same-or-similar repeat breach the tenant may serve a fresh 30-day notice with **no second cure right**. | **General reasonable-accommodation duty** | **Yes — CADA, and it is the most enforceable of the five.** **§24-34-502** makes it a discriminatory housing practice to refuse to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services where necessary to afford a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling; §24-34-502.2 (Unfair Housing Practices) and §24-34-803 supplement it. Enforced by the **Colorado Civil Rights Division** alongside the federal FHA, with **§24-34-309's $3,500-per-plaintiff-per-violation statutory fine** and a private right of action. | **Rent-modification / rent-increase notice** | **Two separate limits, and the frequency cap applies to EVERY tenancy.** §38-12-701(2)(a): in a residential tenancy **with no written agreement**, rent may be increased only on **at least 60 days' written notice** — and (2)(b) bars terminating such a tenancy by notice **with the primary purpose of increasing rent** inconsistently with the section. *Where a written lease exists, no statutory notice period applies; the lease governs.* **§38-12-702 is the broader rule: a landlord shall not increase rent MORE THAN ONCE IN ANY TWELVE-MONTH PERIOD of consecutive occupancy — regardless of whether there is a written agreement, and regardless of whether the tenancy is fixed, month-to-month, or indefinite.** *No other canvassed state limits the FREQUENCY of increases at all; ND and SD regulate only notice, KS and MN not even that directly.* History: part added SB 17-245; §38-12-701 amended HB 21-1121 (2021) and **HB 24-1098 (2024)**. | **Termination notice — periodic tenancy** | **Scales by tenancy length — and since 2024 a residential landlord largely CANNOT use it.** §13-40-107(1) (Title 13, not Title 38): one year or longer **91 days**; six months to a year **28 days**; one to six months **21 days**; one week to one month, or tenancy at will, **3 days**; under one week **1 day**. *Longest periodic-tenancy notice of the five states by a wide margin — SD/ND cap at one month, MN at three, KS fixes 7/30 days.* **HB 24-1098 (ch. 113, eff. 2024-04-19) amended the ENTIRE section** and restricted who may invoke it: as amended, a **landlord of nonresidential property or of a residential premises exempted under §38-12-1302(1)(a),(b),(d),(e),(f)**, or **a tenant of any property**, may terminate a periodic tenancy or decline to renew a fixed term. **For ordinary residential tenancies the landlord must instead proceed under the just-cause regime at §§38-12-1301 et seq. — enumerated cause, or a no-fault ground with 90 days' written notice.** HB 24-1098 also **eliminated** the tenant-at-will presumption and the condominium carve-out. *No other canvassed state has a just-cause requirement; all four permit no-cause termination on notice* | **No statutory notice period — and a widely-repeated 30-day claim rests on a MISCITATION.** Multiple sources state plainly that Wyoming has **no statute** governing notice to terminate a month-to-month, week-to-week, or year-or-longer periodic tenancy; the lease governs. ### How to use this section

**Do not fill a cell from a decision log without checking against primary text first.** This rule produced the original SD-only cells, each backed by primary statutory text read during the SD re-audit with the section number in the cell. The table has since been filled for the other six states too, following the same discipline — each cell's own sourcing note (e.g. "verified from wyoleg.gov," "tiered below the other six," or an explicit "not read from primary text in this pass") tells you how much weight that specific cell can bear. A cell filled straight from a prior log's narrative, without this kind of independent verification, would carry that log's confidence — and this project's re-audit standard is that logs are claims to verify, not facts.

**Expect this section to find errors.** Two of the fourteen SD rows above record provisions that were *wrong or missing in the library* until the SD re-audit: the deposit-return deadline had shipped a superseded figure for over two months, and the state reasonable-accommodation duty was absent entirely. Both are universal obligations. That hit rate on the first state canvassed is the argument for running the other six.

**Sequencing note.** These topics are cheap to canvass — each is a single well-known provision in every state — but they are load-bearing, since most appear in `REQUIRED` clauses that ship into every generated lease. They should rank above further exotic-topic discovery.

| **Core tenant-protection statute on a dated repeal clock** | **Present.** §§1946.2(n) and 1947.12(o): both repeal 2030-01-01. Four CA rows lapse together (`edu-tpa-sunset-ca`) | **Yes.** A sunset is invisible to ordinary bill-tracking until an extension bill appears. Screen every state's core protections for a sunset subdivision and route hits to the legal-watch workflow |
| **A dormant row asserting a self-repealed statute** | **Present — `foreclosure-disclosure-ca`.** Civ. Code §2924.85 was enacted by an act titled "to **add and repeal**" it and self-repealed 2018-01-01. The library carried the duty as live for eight years | **Yes — this is a new error shape, adjacent to Instruction 17.** That instruction warns against citing a bill that was never enacted; this is the mirror image, an enacted statute that expired. Any "add and repeal" enacting title is a sunset signal. Add to the citation-existence screen: confirm the section is not only real but still **operative** |
| **Water submeter billing — prescribed disclosure, billing limits and late-fee cap** | **Present, prescribed, and the largest single gap this backfill found.** Civ. Code Chapter 2.5 (commencing with §1954.201), operative 2018-01-01 (§1954.218). **§1954.204**: a landlord who intends to charge separately from rent for water service in a property with submeters must disclose **ten** listed items **in writing, in at least 10-point type, before executing the rental agreement**, and the statute expressly allows them to be "incorporated into the rental agreement." **§1954.205** is a closed list of billable items. **§1954.206** sets read and due-date timing, an eleven-item bill-content list, and bars requiring electronic payment. **§1954.213** is the operative surprise: no late fee until **25 days** after the bill is sent; **$7** first bill, **$10** each subsequent; all late fees in any 12-month period capped at **10 percent** of the unpaid amount; partial payments to the **oldest** bill; termination only at **180 days overdue or $200 unpaid**, and then by a **three-day notice to perform covenants or quit**; **water charges are not rent**; and **no shutoff for any reason including nonpayment** — an absolute bar, unlike Civ. Code §789.3 which needs intent to terminate the occupancy. **§1954.214** preserves pre-2013 local ordinances. `water-submeter-disclosure-ca`, `edu-water-submeter-billing-ca`. Not read: §§1954.203, 1954.207–1954.212, 1954.215–1954.217, 1954.219; Water Code §§537–537.5; PUC §739.5. (backfill 2026-09-28) | YES — high priority. Ratio-utility and submetered billing is common everywhere and this library has no row for it in any state. |
| **Towing a vehicle from the property — signage and authorization** | **Present and highly prescriptive.** Veh. Code **§22658**, read section-open for subdivisions (a), (e)(1) and (l)(1)(A) (the section runs ~23,000 characters; the rest was not read). Removal without the vehicle owner's consent needs a sign **at least 17 × 22 inches**, lettering **at least 1 inch**, in plain view **at all entrances**, prohibiting public parking, stating removal at the owner's expense, and giving the local traffic law enforcement number **plus the name and number of every towing company under a written general towing authorization agreement** — so changing tow companies means changing every sign. Alternatives: 96 hours after a parking-violation notice; 24 hours after notifying law enforcement about a vehicle lacking a major part. **A parcel improved with a single-family dwelling needs no sign.** Non-compliance makes the authorising owner liable for **double** the towing or storage charges (§22658(e)(1)). Separately, the towing company needs the owner's or lessee's **written authorization** and the authoriser must normally **be present and verify**, with a carve-out for a **residential rental property of 15 or fewer units** with no onsite staff where the **tenant** verifies and requests the tow from that tenant's own assigned space. `edu-towing-ca`. (backfill 2026-09-28) | YES. Arizona's screen found the same gap (`edu-towing-az`); two of fourteen states now have a row. |
| **Selling or refinancing a tenanted property — showings, deposit transfer, disclosure currency, estoppel** | **Present, in four separate duties, none of which had a row.** Civ. Code **§1954(d)(2)**: after written notice within the previous 120 days that the property is for sale, entry to show it may be arranged on **oral** notice, with **written evidence of the entry left in the unit**. **§1950.5(i)**: on transfer, either hand the remaining deposit to the successor and then notify the tenant in writing of the transfer, the claims made, the amount and the successor's name, address and telephone number, or return it with a full accounting. **§1950.5(j)**: before a voluntary transfer, give the buyer a written statement of the remaining deposit, an itemisation of lawful deductions and the route elected. **§1950.5(k)**: joint and several liability for non-compliance, with a good-faith shelter for the successor at (k)(3). **§1962(c)**: the identity disclosure must be kept current, binds the successor within 15 days, and a non-compliant successor **may not serve a CCP §1161(2) nonpayment notice** for rent accrued during noncompliance. **Estoppel certificates are confirmed absent statute-wide** ("estoppel certificate" and "tenant estoppel" each return 0 sections), so a tenant may refuse the certification both professional forms demand. `edu-selling-rented-property-ca`. (backfill 2026-09-28) | YES. Arizona has `edu-selling-rented-property-az`; this is the second. |
| **Holding deposits and money taken before the lease** | **Confirmed absent code-wide as a distinct rule, and that is the trap.** Official leginfo search, all codes: "holding deposit" 4 sections (none landlord-tenant), "application deposit" **0**, "reservation deposit" 1 (Fin. Code §17312). The governing sections are the ones already read: Civ. Code **§1950.5(b)** defines security as any payment, fee, deposit or charge imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to reimburse processing a new tenant or as an advance payment of rent, used for any purpose, **"however denominated"**; **§1950.5(c)(1)** caps it at one month; **§1950.5(n)** forbids characterising security as non-refundable; and **§1950.6(k)** makes the application screening fee the one thing that is **neither** security **nor** an advance fee, with §1950.6(j) extending "applicant" to **guarantors and cosigners**. So calling money a non-refundable holding fee does not make it one. **Open:** whether §1950.5(b) reaches money taken before a tenancy begins at all, given its own words "at the beginning of the tenancy" — the statutes do not settle it and no case was read. `edu-holding-deposit-ca`. (backfill 2026-09-28) | YES. Arizona has `edu-holding-deposit-az`. |
| **Tenant-installed security cameras and video doorbells** | **Confirmed absent from the California codes 2026-09-28.** Official leginfo search, all codes: "security camera" returns 3 sections (Educ. Code §49005.8, Rev. & Tax. Code §§17053.64, 23664), none landlord-tenant; "video doorbell" returns **0**. Neither a tenant's right to install nor a landlord's right to refuse is regulated by statute, so it is a lease-drafting matter. The CAA CA-041 12/24 form addresses it by requiring the landlord's prior written consent for any device capturing images or sound outside the unit. **Scope limit, stated:** Penal Code §§632 and 647(j) regulate *recording* rather than installation and were not searched under those terms, and no case law was read — so this is an absence of an installation rule, not a conclusion that recording is unregulated. No row. (backfill 2026-09-28) | YES — a modern recurring question with no row anywhere in the library. |
| **Satellite dishes and over-the-air antennas** | **Confirmed absent from the California codes 2026-09-28.** "satellite dish" returns 2 sections, both common interest development — Civ. Code §4725 (residential CIDs) and §6708 (commercial). There is **no landlord-tenant statute**, and the rule that actually governs is the **federal FCC OTARD rule, 47 C.F.R. §1.4000, which was not read.** So the honest record is: no California statute, and the controlling authority is federal and unexamined. Where the property is in a CID, §4725 and `hoa-compliance` apply. No row. (backfill 2026-09-28) | YES, but as a single federal question — OTARD is federal and preempts inconsistent lease restrictions in every state, so one read would answer it for all fourteen rather than fourteen separate screens. |

### CA answers to the CO/KS/NE re-audit rows that have no CA column — 2026-09-19

| Re-audit row | CA |
|---|---|
| **Trained service animal: independent state basis** | **Present — regulatory, and species-open.** 2 CCR §12005(d)(1) + §12185(b): service animals permitted in all dwellings *including common and public use areas*. Service animals **need not be professionally trained or certified** and may be trained by the individual with the disability — broader than NE's training-gated 2008 C.F.R. freeze — and **not limited to dogs**, unlike KS |
| **ESA specifically: independent state basis** | **Present — the strongest answer in the project, and it reveals a FIFTH classification category.** 2 CCR §12005(d) expressly includes **support animals** providing emotional, cognitive or similar support; §12185(c) gives them a reasonable-accommodation route. The basis is neither an independent animal-specific *statute* nor a merely generic accommodation duty — it is an **independent, animal-specific ADMINISTRATIVE REGULATION** under a generic statute (authority Gov. Code §12935(a); reference §§12920, 12921, 12926, 12926.1, 12927, 12955, 12955.3 and *Auburn Woods I HOA v. FEHC* (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 1578). **Survives the HUD withdrawal completely** — it never rested on HUD guidance. Operative 2020-01-01. **The four-way classification should become five-way** |
| **Landlord-facing criminal penalty for DENYING an assistance animal** | **Not located.** 2 CCR §12185 states no penalty. FEHA's remedial provisions and Civ. Code §54.3 were not read, so this is *not located*, not confirmed absent |

**Additional CA topic — an administrative-code basis for a REQUIRED clause family.**
CA joins KS (K.A.R.), ND (Admin. Code), SD (ARSD) and OH (OAC 4112-5-07(C)) in placing assistance-animal
rights in regulation rather than statute — but CA is the first where the regulation is the *primary and most
detailed* source rather than a gloss on a statute. **Instruction 16 flag:** agency rulemaking is invisible to
legislative bill-tracking, so the legal-watch workflow needs a Civil Rights Council rulemaking watch
distinct from its bill watch. Five states now depend on this.

**Scope trap worth recording (the WY/MN pattern, third occurrence).**
2 CCR §14331 is a near-identical assistance-animal regulation sitting in the state-programs / covered-entities
article, **not housing**. Its text is seductive — it contains the breed/size/weight bar and the direct-threat
standard almost verbatim — and citing it for a lease would be the same error as citing KS's public-
accommodations place-list provision for housing. **§12185 is the housing rule.**

### Further topics California surfaced later in the pass — added 2026-09-19

The rows above were written early. These emerged from the statutory walk, the extend screen and the
citation screen, and are the ones the next state should carry forward.

| Topic | CA | Check for other states? |
|---|---|---|
| **Opt-in landlord rights — promote from a CO curiosity to a STANDING QUESTION** | **Seven confirmed in one state.** §1946.2(b)(2)(A)(ii) owner move-in · CCP §1174(c) forfeiture clause (include one and lose the tenant's mandatory five-day redemption window) · §827(a) seven-day terms-change notice · §1942.1's arbitration limb (only if the lease sets forth §§1941–1942.1) · §1951.2(c)(1) balance-of-term damages · §1951.2(b) interest rate · §1951.4(a) continue-the-lease remedy, which ships **safe-harbour wording** in the statute. One suspected and unresolved: §1951.2(e) indemnification | **Yes — ask it of every state, every time.** CO raised it as a single provision; CA shows it can be a pervasive drafting architecture. The right canvass question is *which landlord rights does this state condition on the lease saying so?* — not *does this state have an analogue to C.R.S. 38-12-503(11)?* |
| **Self-defeating clauses — lawful, but they forfeit a remedy** | **Present: `no-sublet-assign`.** A sole-discretion consent requirement is perfectly lawful in a CA residential lease, and the extend screen cleared it on that basis. But §1951.4(b) makes the continue-the-lease remedy available only where the lease permits sublet/assignment, or sets reasonable express standards, or requires consent not unreasonably withheld. Sole discretion satisfies none — so the clause silently costs the landlord a remedy | **Yes, and it is a new DEFECT SHAPE.** Every prior screen asked "is this clause void or unlawful?" This one is neither. A clause can be fully enforceable and still be the wrong choice because a statute conditions a benefit on drafting it differently. Screens keyed to voidness will never catch it |
| **Cross-reference rot — a real, operative citation that points at the wrong text** | **Two instances.** 2 CCR §12185(c)(2) cites "§12178(f)" for reliable third-party information; §12178(f) is the *self-certification* provision — §12185 was filed 2019 and never amended, §12178 was amended operative 2022, and a re-lettering would strand the pointer. Worse: CCP §1161(4) still cites **Civ. Code §3485**, repealed 2024-01-01 — and §1161 was itself amended by SB 611 in 2024 **without fixing it** | **Yes.** Distinct from every catalogued shape: the cite is real, operative and correctly transcribed, and still lands on the wrong text. **A recently-amended statute is not evidence its cross-references are current.** Flag divergent amendment dates between a citing and a cited section. And quote the source as written, footnoting the discrepancy, rather than silently "correcting" it |
| **"The citation resolves but the duty doesn't exist" — three distinct mechanisms** | **All three in one state.** *Repealed by its own terms* — §2924.85, sunset 2018-01-01, and an "add and repeal" enacting title is the tell. *Spent one-time limb* — §1954.603's duty to notify all existing tenants by 2018-01-01, discharged and not modellable. *Never commenced* — H&S §26147(e) suspends the section until predicate standards are adopted | **Yes — extend the citation screen's question.** It currently asks "does this section exist?" It should ask **"is this section operative?"** Two flags: an "add and repeal" enacting title, and a contingent-commencement subdivision |
| **State law geographically confined to named cities** | **Present.** Civ. Code §3486 is a Civil Code section that operates **only in the City of Los Angeles** (§3486(g)); repealed §3485 covered LA, Long Beach, Sacramento and Oakland. Both are incorporated into CCP §1161(4)'s deemed-nuisance list, so that limb is one statewide ground, one city-only ground and a dead pointer | **Yes, and it breaks the municipal scope boundary.** The project draws that boundary around *ordinances*. This is state law that applies in some cities and not others — inside the boundary by its source, outside it by its effect. A state-level-only pass will silently over-generalise it |
| **The same prohibition enacted twice, in two codes** | **Present: the notice-service fee ban.** Civ. Code §1946.1(i) covers §1946.1 notices; CCP §1161(6) separately covers the three-day notice family, added by SB 611 operative 2025-02-01 | **Yes.** A canvass that finds one and stops will mis-scope the rule — I nearly did, recording a scope caution on §1946.1(i) that §1161(6) later resolved |
| **Document-TIMING rules — void because of *when* the lease changed hands** | **Present: §1953(b).** Any provision modifying or waiving a statutory right, not already void under §1953(a), §1942.1, §1942.5 or §1954, is void **unless the lease was presented to the tenant before the tenant took actual possession**. Renewals carrying the same provision forward are carved out | **Yes, and no clause-level screen can catch it.** Every screen in this project reads clause text. This one turns on a fact about delivery. It is app behaviour, not drafting — the builder needs to know whether the lease was delivered pre-possession |
| **Tenant-screening regulation as a distinct area** | **Present and untouched.** Civ. Code §1950.6 (fee, CPI-indexed from a 1998 base, plus a mandatory choice between two screening processes) and §1950.1 (reusable reports — accepting them forfeits the screening fee entirely). §1950.1(f) points at **2 CCR Art. 24, §12264 et seq.**, Civil Rights Council rules on considering criminal history in housing, **not read** | **Yes — this is a canvass GAP, not just a CA gap.** Screening sits upstream of the lease and the canvass has no row for it in any state. Add one |
| **Administrative code as the PRIMARY source for a REQUIRED family** | **Present.** 2 CCR §§12005(d), 12176–12181, 12185 are the primary and most detailed source of CA's assistance-animal and accommodation rules — not a gloss on a statute. Five states now depend on agency rules for a REQUIRED family (KS, ND, SD, OH, CA) | **Yes — and it is a legal-watch design requirement.** Agency rulemaking is invisible to legislative bill-tracking. The watch workflow needs a rulemaking watch (here, the Civil Rights Council) distinct from its bill watch |
| **Multiple type-size floors and translation duties in one state** | **Five type-size floors:** 8-point (§2079.10a, Gov. Code §8589.45), 10-point (§1954.603), 12-point (§1946.2(f)(3)), 14-point bold (§3486(a)(1)(C), prosecutor's notice). **Three §1632 linkages**, and §1632 itself requires a **full translated lease** — every term and condition — on any tenancy longer than one month, with **rescission** as the remedy | **Yes, and it is a SCHEMA gap.** The schema can express neither a minimum type size nor "this lease must also exist in another language." Four required CA clauses depend on the first, two on the second |

Code §§400–409.15)** | A complete state SCRA analog: definitions (§400); chain-of-command and waiver rules (§401); default-judgment declaration with a **120-day lookback** (§402); stays of action and writ (§403); **eviction of a service member's dependents barred absent leave of court** (§406); **lease termination** (§409); storage-lien bar (§409.1); dependents' standing (§409.5); **30-day written-response duty on any relief request, on pain of waiver** (§409.15). Whether narrower or broader than the federal SCRA: **not assessed**, federal statute not read. `military-lease-termination-ca` (moved to `edu-military-tenant-protections-ca` by the 2026-09-29 scrub), `edu-military-default-judgment-ca`, `edu-military-tenant-protections-ca` |
| 294.10 | Is the cited rent-increase notice actually the mobile-home rule? | **No** | §827 is general. Mobilehome tenancies have their own regime (§798 et seq.) and §§1946.2(l), 1947.12(j) exclude mobilehome homeowners. |
| 335.1 / 367.8 | Cash rent payment receipt duty | **Present — on request, not automatic** | **Civ. Code §1499:** a debtor may *require* a written receipt for any payment. On request and for every form of payment — not an automatic cash-receipt duty like Minnesota's. `owner-identity-disclosure-ca` |
| 335.2 / 367.9 | Lease copy delivery duty — and failure as a defence | **Present — CORRECTED** | **CORRECTED 2026-09-19.** I first entered this as 'not checked — verify §1962' without checking my own CSV; §1962 had already been read and rowed. **§1962(a)(4):** copy of the lease within **15 days** of the tenant signing, and once a year on request within 15 days. **As a defence:** no general defence for the original owner, but **§1962(c)** bars a *successor* owner or manager who has not complied within 15 days from serving a pay-or-quit or evicting for nonpayment of rent accrued during the noncompliance. `owner-identity-disclosure-ca` |
| 335.3 | Inspection statute notice duty distinct from inspection | **Present** | §1950.5(f)(1): written notice of the tenant's right to request an initial inspection, and 48 hours' written notice of its date. `security-deposit-return-ca` (moved to `edu-security-deposit-return-ca` by the 2026-09-29 scrub) |
| 335.4 | Two-track abandoned property keyed to storage location | **Single track; location affects cost only** | §1986 property left on premises or stored; §1990(c) on-premises storage priced at fair rental value, no charge if reclaimed within two days. `edu-abandoned-property-ca` |
| 335.5 / 367.6 | Does a disclosure failure bar the eviction itself? | **YES — two mechanisms** | §1946.2(g): failure to comply with any provision of §1946.2, including the (f) lease disclosure, **voids** the termination notice. **And §1962(c):** a successor owner who has not given the §1962 identity disclosures may not evict for nonpayment of rent accrued during the noncompliance. `tpa-notice-ca`, `owner-identity-disclosure-ca` |
| 335.6 / 367.10 | Landlord duty to mitigate on early termination | **Present, burden on tenant** | §1951.2(a)(2)–(3): landlord recovers loss less what the LESSEE PROVES could reasonably have been avoided; §1951.2(d) mitigation efforts don't waive damages. `early-termination-ca` |
| 335.7 | Does one tenant's protected termination end the lease for ALL? | **No** | §1946.7(g): other tenants remain bound — same as ND, opposite of MN. |
| 335.8 | Statutory forms supplied verbatim | **Present — richest in project** | §§1946.2(f)(3), 1946.2(e)(8)(B)(i), 1946.7(b)(3)(B), 1941.5(d)(3), 1941.1(a)(11)(B)(i), 1951.3(e), 1984, 1985, 1940.8.5, 1954.071, 2079.10a, 1947.3(a)(3)(C), H&S §8589.45, 2924.8. |
| 335.9 | Lease LAYOUT requirements | **Present** | §1945.5: auto-renewal in 8-point bold plus a recital immediately above the signature. Plus seven type-size floors. `auto-renewal-formatting-ca` |
| 367.1 | Self-help eviction / unlawful ouster ban and money remedy | **Present — READ 2026-09-19** | **Civ. Code §789.3(b):** no lockout, bootlock, removal of outside doors or windows, or removal of belongings without prior written consent (except via the §1980 procedure), where done willfully with intent to terminate occupancy. Actual damages **plus up to $100 per day, minimum $250 per separate cause of action**; non-contemporaneous repeats are separate causes; prevailing-party fees and injunctive relief. Sits in Division 2 — outside Title 5, which is why the chapter sweep missed it. `edu-self-help-eviction-ban-ca` |
| 367.2 | Willful utility shutoff as a distinct violation | **Present — READ 2026-09-19** | **Civ. Code §789.3(a):** willfully causing interruption of any utility — water, heat, light, electricity, gas, telephone, elevator, refrigeration — with intent to terminate occupancy, **whether or not the landlord controls the utility**, so causing a shutoff *indirectly* is covered. Same remedy as 367.1. `edu-self-help-eviction-ban-ca` |
| 367.3 | Post-writ tenant property duties | **Present — read in full** | **CCP §1174(e)–(m)** via **§715.030**: 15 days to reclaim on paying storage; lost property to police; non-tenant owners noticed under §1983; disposal under §1988 with liability shields. §1174(h)'s reference to Civ. Code §1965 not read. Service-member storage liens need a court order (Mil. & Vet. §409.1(b)). `edu-writ-execution-ca` |
| 367.4 | Post-writ PET ANIMAL duties | **Routed elsewhere** | §1981(d) excludes animals from the abandoned-property chapter and sends them to Civ. Code §1815 or Food & Ag. Code §17001 et seq. — neither read. |
| 367.5 | Writ execution timing constraints | **Present** | **CCP §715.020(c):** five days after service, **no extension** (§684.120 disapplied); §715.040 process server may execute if the sheriff hasn't in three court days; **§715.050: tenant bankruptcy does not delay the possession writ.** No daylight-only or SSI/SSDI rule found. `edu-writ-execution-ca` |
| 367.7 | Holdover damages figure vs shared clause | **Checked** | `holdover-ca` override built; §1951.5 confirms §1671 governs any liquidated figure. |
| 427.1 | Does the DV definition limit the PERPETRATOR class? | **No limit** | §1946.7(a) reaches any perpetrator of the listed acts; §§1941.5 and 1941.6 split by whether the perpetrator is a co-tenant, not by relationship. `dv-lease-termination-ca` (moved to `edu-abuse-violence-protections-ca` by the 2026-09-29 scrub) |
| 427.2 | Escheat: landlord as statutory holder | **Present — landlord is a holder** | **CCP §1520(a):** intangible property owed in the ordinary course of business and unclaimed **more than three years** escheats; **§1530(d):** annual report before **November 1**. An unclaimed deposit refund makes the landlord a holder. Pre-escheat notice, penalties and interest provisions not read in full. `edu-deposit-escheat-ca` |
| 427.3 | Dormancy charge as a drafting hook | **Resolved — dormancy charge BARRED** | The opposite of North Dakota. **CCP §1522** bars deducting any charge imposed *because of* inactive or unclaimed status unless this chapter specifically permits it, and the only permitted charge is the **$2** pre-escheat notice fee (§1520(b)). A lease-created dormancy charge doesn't work. `edu-deposit-escheat-ca` |

The real traps are elsewhere — the stop-payment good-faith-dispute rule, bank-error and delayed-benefit exceptions, and a certified-mail demand that unlocks **treble damages ($100–$1,500)**. `nsf-fee-limit-ca` |

The correct reference is §1946.7(h)(5). The prescribed form itself carries the error; ship it verbatim but note it. |
| 427.8 | Two-limb portfolio exemptions read conjunctively | **Present, repeatedly** | §1950.5(c)(5)(A)(i)–(ii) both required; §1954.07(j)(1)(A)–(B); §1946.2(e)(8)(A)–(B); §1947.12(d)(5). |
| 551.1–551.5 | Missing core topics (deposit return, habitability, assistance animal, meth, M2M notice) | **All present** | `security-deposit-return-ca` (moved to `edu-security-deposit-return-ca` by the 2026-09-29 scrub), habitability rows, `assistance-animal-accommodation-ca`, `meth-disclosure-ca`, `month-to-month-notice-ca`. |
| 572.1 | Flag display as a lease restriction | **Not located** | Title 5 protects political signs (§1940.4) and religious items (§1940.45); no flag-display provision found in Title 5. |

| 572.4 | Mandatory eviction as a landlord DUTY | **Not a duty — prosecutor route** | §3486 lets a city prosecutor require the owner to act or assign; no freestanding landlord duty to evict. `edu-nuisance-eviction-assignment-ca` |
| 572.5 | Verbatim statutory notice wording | **Present** | See 335.8. |

Code §290.46(j)(2)(G) prohibits using Megan's Law website information for housing or accommodations**, except to protect a person at risk — actual damages, up to 3x, **$250 minimum**, fees, exemplary damages or a civil penalty up to **$25,000**. The reverse of Ohio's §5321.051. And §2079.10a still requires the lease to tell tenants the site exists. Parolee residency limits (Pen. Code §3003.5) not read. `edu-megans-law-housing-use-ca` |
| 572.7 | Fair-housing election right to the respondent | **No — CA housing enforcement is judicial** | No respondent election right, because there is no administrative forum to elect out of: the department prosecutes housing cases by **civil action in superior court** (Gov. Code §12981(a)(1)). From 2026, **mandatory dispute resolution** for all parties first (§12981(a)(2), SB 477). Private action within 2 years with punitive damages; AG penalties up to $50,000 / $100,000. `edu-fair-housing-classes-ca` |

**Tally: 86 refs.** Answered: 70 (including one N/A, no source-of-income class; escheat, dormancy and respondent election added after the gap searches later the same day). Not located: 15. Not checked: 0. Not a state-law question: 1 (ACH). **Two findings worth carrying to other states:**
- **294.7:** check whether the state's animal rule is keyed to the fair-housing "dwelling" definition or to the landlord-tenant chapter's coverage.
- **694.1:** Nevada's named-repairer option (§118A.360(2)) is the kind of opt-in right CA said to screen for.

**New topic from the Nevada gap searches (2026-09-24):** **statute versions whose effective date is contingent on a federal certification.** NRS 233.160 exists in two versions. The housing-specific one, with NRS 233.165–.170, takes effect only when the Governor declares Nevada's housing law substantially equivalent to federal law. A drafter reading the wrong version would describe a process that is not in force. **Check for other states? Yes** — look for "[Effective on the date …]" bracket notes.

**Tally: 104 refs.** Answered: 76. Not located: 26. Not checked: 0 (dormancy charges — service-charge sections of Prop. Code chs. 72–74 not retrieved). N/A: 2.

**Findings worth carrying to other states:**
- **134.5** — statutory fee *reciprocity*: Texas makes a one-way landlord fee clause mutual in eviction suits (§24.006(c)). Check whether the shared prevailing-party wording is doing any work in states with a similar rule.
- **294.7** — Texas's small-owner fair-housing exemption also removes the *state* accommodation duty, because the duty sits inside the exempted section. Nevada's did not. Worth one line in each state's fair-housing row.
- **335.2** — a lease-copy failure can abate the landlord's non-rent lawsuits (§92.024(d)). The first "disclosure failure bars enforcement" finding since MN's §504B.181.
- **694.1** — Texas has the most opt-in landlord rights of any state so far; instruction 30 now asks for the list explicitly.

## Texas scope and status notes (2026-09-25)

- **One careful pass, then a mechanical cross-check**, per instruction 22 (correct settings from the start, so not a second audit). The cross-check was instruction 19: all 67 row ids named in the TX answers were checked against `lease-clauses.csv`. 65 are active TX rows. The other 2 are deliberate references to rows not tagged TX (`security-devices-ca` as the CA precedent; base `holdover`, named as not tagged).
- **Proof of absence (Taylor ran the official site's full-text search):** radon, bed bugs, mold, carbon-monoxide alarms and meth are CONFIRMED ABSENT at statute level; immigration-status rules, EV charging and a rent-increase notice statute are CONFIRMED ABSENT within the Property Code. The search matches exact word forms only (confirmed with a "rental increases" control), so every absence was searched in its variant forms. Each topic has its own row.
- **Municipal layer:** flagged, not resolved (instruction 20). Texas's state preemption is itself a finding (§24.0043, §§92.170, 92.208, 92.252; Loc. Gov't Code §§214.902, 250.007); HB 2127 not read.
- **Open:** nothing required. Judgment calls for Taylor are in the TX log (§18): whether to write any clause for S.B. 17 leases of a year or more.

**Findings worth carrying to other states:**
- **335.5** — registration as a bar to a possession judgment (N.J.S.A. 46:8-33). This is the third "disclosure failure bars enforcement" finding, after MN §504B.181 and TX §92.024(d).
- **335.7** — one tenant's DV termination ends the lease for all co-tenants (N.J.S.A. 46:8-9.7(c)). Texas was silent on this.
- **134.5** — second state with automatic fee reciprocity, and the first to require the reciprocity sentence *in the lease*.
- **294.7** — the LAD small-owner exemption (10:5-5(n)) and the service-dog housing rule ("all housing accommodations", 10:5-29.2) may not align. Unresolved.

## Florida scope and status notes (2026-09-26)

- **Scope:** state law only. Municipal and county ordinances flagged, not resolved (instruction 20). Florida's §83.425 preemption makes the local layer thinner than in NJ or TX, but which local rules survive is an open research question (`edu-local-preemption-fl`).
- **Settings:** Opus, high effort, ordinary search and fetch; research mode not used. No proof-of-absence searches were run, so every 'Not located' stays bounded.
- **Research-mode pass (2026-09-26, once):** settled the §83.425 dates and reach (pre-existing ordinances included), corrected ch. 2024-27 (towing only), left local fair-housing ordinance survival UNSETTLED (no court or AG authority exists), read §83.684. It did NOT run official full-text searches, so no 'Not located' was upgraded. Immigration: SB 1718 (2023) imposes no landlord duty per secondary sources; not a verified absence.
- **Proof-of-absence searches (Taylor, 2026-09-26):** all CONFIRMED ABSENT (statutes): mold, bed bugs, eviction-record sealing, domestic-violence lease termination, immigration status, EV charging, deposit cap, late-fee and application-fee caps. Quoted phrase plus a second word narrows results; subject-index hits are pointers, not law.
- **Instruction 19:** 45 row ids named in the FL cells and sections were checked against the CSV: 43 are active FL rows; 2 (`default-by-tenant`, `common-area-use`) are deliberate references to base rows Florida overrides.
- **New standing instructions:** 33 (cure promise vs no-cure grounds) and 34 (session-law effective dates).
- **Gap-discovery backfill (2026-09-27):** sources 2 (Florida Realtors RLHD-3x lease) and 3 (69-scenario screen) were run as a targeted, one-time check (FL log, gap-discovery backfill section); its status table shows all four instruction-36 sources done for FL. 8 new rows; 3 body additions and 1 note-only change, all to FL-only rows. Confirmed absent (statutes), from Taylor's official full-text searches: holding deposit, rent-increase notice, cash-rent receipt, pool-safety notice to tenants, utility shutoff notice for master-metered buildings, and lease termination on the tenant's death. Out of scope: condominium conversion (§718.606, developer duties). Flagged: medical-marijuana limits on smoking bans (existing `smoking-policy` note) and the foreign-principal buyer (TX1.19).

| **Statute lets the landlord amend existing leases by written notice to comply with new laws, which a shared 'signed writing only' clause can give up** | **Present** - A.R.S. §33-1342(C); shared `entire-agreement` edited for all states (uniform, AZ log §14) | Yes |
| **Statutory ban on passing a repealed local tax through to tenants, with the burden of proof on the landlord** | **Present** - A.R.S. §33-1332 (through 2026-12-31); §42-6004(H); former §33-1314(E) deleted - `edu-rental-tax-az` | Yes |
| **Criminal trespass for staying or returning after a writ of restitution** | **Present** - A.R.S. §12-1178(D)-(E) | Yes |
| **Courts and agencies barred from requiring a mandatory or technical notice or pleading form** | **Present** - A.R.S. §§33-1305(C), 33-361(F), 12-1175(D) | Yes |
| **State statute extends federal servicemember civil-relief protections to Guard and reserve members on STATE orders, outside the landlord-tenant title** | **Present** - A.R.S. §26-168(D); reach to current SCRA lease termination not determined - `edu-no-servicemember-lease-rule-az` (found through the AAR form comparison, AZ log §16) | Yes |
| **Holding deposit or earnest money taken before the lease is signed** | **Confirmed absent (statutes)** as a specific rule; the §33-1321(A) cap and §33-1321(B) nonrefundable-designation rule bear on it; brokers must state the earnest money's form (§32-2151.01(C)) - `edu-holding-deposit-az` | Yes TX (backfill 2026-09-27): Present as the 'application deposit' (§§92.351–.355; refund on rejection); `edu-rental-application-tx`. NE (backfill 2026-09-27): **Confirmed absent.** `holding deposit` 58 hits (all banking), `holding fee` 101 (all licensing and permit fees). Nothing regulates a pre-lease holding or reservation deposit, its permitted uses, or refundability if the applicant withdraws. The written agreement is the only governing instrument. `edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-ne`. MN (backfill 2026-09-27): **Present, and stricter than any state so far.** §504B.175: a prelease deposit may be accepted only under a CONSPICUOUS WRITTEN agreement stating the circumstances of return and the seven-day return duty; "return" means postmarked within seven days; if a lease is signed the money MUST be applied to the security deposit or rent; remedy is the deposit PLUS one-half as a penalty. A reasonable applicant screening fee is expressly excluded from the definition, so §§504B.173 and 504B.175 govern different money (`edu-prelease-deposit-mn`, `prelease-deposit-application-mn` (moved to `edu-prelease-deposit-mn` by the 2026-09-29 scrub)). Contrast AZ, where the topic is a confirmed statutory absence. |
| **Mandatory security devices and rekey at turnover (TX topic; AZ answer from the AAR comparison)** | **Confirmed absent (statutes)** - full-text search: rekey/re-key variants hit only §33-1318 (victim lock change); deadbolt, door lock(s), change the locks: 0 (AZ log §16) | Yes MN (backfill 2026-09-27): Confirmed absent. "rekey" 0, "deadbolt" 0, "door lock" 1 (§326B.124, construction-code exemptions), "change the locks" 1 (§582.031 — a MORTGAGEE's limited right of entry during foreclosure, not a landlord duty). No rekey, deadbolt or lock-hardware duty. The only statutory lock rule runs the other way: the victim lock-change right (`edu-no-rekey-or-lock-duty-mn`). Matches AZ; contrast TX §92.156 et seq. |
| **Fire sprinklers in rentals** | **No landlord duty located**; §§9-807, 11-861 bar cities and counties from mandating sprinklers in single-family detached or two-unit residences (post-2009 codes) (AZ log §16) | Yes |
| **Towing from private rental property: written tow authorization and (in cities) mandatory parking signs** | **Present** - A.R.S. §§9-499.05(B)-(C), 11-251.04(C); outside the landlord-tenant title - `edu-towing-az` (landlord-experience screen, AZ log §18) | Yes TX (backfill 2026-09-27): Present — Occ. Code ch. 2308; `edu-private-property-towing-tx`. SD (backfill 2026-09-28): Present, structurally different (landowner **or tenant** written permission, no signage; SDCL 32-36-4.1) — `edu-private-property-towing-sd`. MN (backfill 2026-09-27): Present, in Ch. 168B, not the landlord-tenant chapter. §168B.04 subd. 2(b)(2): a vehicle may be impounded from private property immediately where single-family or duplex residential; immediately from ANY residential property PROPERLY POSTED; immediately from posted non-residential; 24 hours from non-residential NOT posted. There is no clause for unposted multi-unit residential — so post the lot. §168B.035 governs government towing authorities and expressly preserves the private owner's authority (subd. 5). §168B.045's towing/storage lien arises only on a LAW-ENFORCEMENT-requested tow. "Properly posted" is used but never defined in §168B.011 (`edu-towing-mn`). Different architecture from AZ's written-authorization-and-signage rule — do not import either way. |
| **Selling landlord released only after written notice of the sale; stays liable for the deposit** | **Present** - A.R.S. §33-1325 - `edu-selling-rented-property-az` (AZ log §18) | Yes TX (backfill 2026-09-27): deposit succession only (§92.105: the buyer is liable from title; the seller stays liable until the buyer takes or assumes the deposits); no general release rule located in ch. 92. SD (backfill 2026-09-28): confirmed absent as a codified rule; no notice-of-sale duty; common law not searched — `edu-deposit-on-sale-sd`. KS (backfill 2026-09-27): **Present** (K.S.A. 58-2554) — `identity-change-liability-ks`. MN (backfill 2026-09-27): Confirmed absent. No analog to AZ §33-1325. Searches: "sells the property" 1, "successor in interest" 45, "right of first refusal" 17 — the only landlord-tenant hits are §504B.178 (deposit transfer and successor liability, already covered) and §504B.285. No notice-of-sale duty and no residential right of first refusal. Whether a buyer takes subject to the tenancy is common law and was not researched (`edu-no-sale-or-successor-duty-mn`). |
| **Tenant duty to give notice of an extended absence (URLTA-style)** | **Confirmed absent (statutes)** - 'extended absence', 'anticipated extended absence': 0 hits; 'absence of the tenant' only §33-1370 (abandonment) (AZ log §18) | Yes TX (backfill 2026-09-27): **Confirmed absent (statutes)** — the phrase 'extended absence' returned 0 hits. KS (backfill 2026-09-27): **Present** (K.S.A. 58-2558) — one of the few places Kansas is stricter than AZ. |
| **Landlord must give a receipt for cash rent** | **Confirmed absent (statutes)** - 'receipt for cash' 0; 'written receipt' and 'cash payment' hits are non-housing (AZ log §18) | Yes KS (backfill 2026-09-27): **Confirmed absent**, full section-index read (58-2549 is titled 'Receipt of rent' but is an anti-waiver rule, not a receipt duty). |
| **Bedbug and similar exclusions keyed to a 'single family residence' definition that includes attached units** | **Present** - A.R.S. §§33-1310(16), 33-1319(D) | Yes |
